weeks.title: Setup + measurement
weeks.theme: Before you train anything you need a frozen dataset, a verifier you trust, and a measured noise floor, or no later gain can be told apart from noise.
goals: Two pinned uv envs (envs/jax with jax[cuda13], flax NNX, optax, orbax, tunix, qwix; envs/torch with vLLM) that never share a process, with allocator settings recorded (PREALLOCATE=false only for dev and parity runs; MEM_FRACTION otherwise) and the persistent compilation cache on (JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR in flake.nix); TRC application and the GCP quota request for the week-11 slice type and region filed

data/splits.json frozen: train 274 / dev 200 (MBPP validation 90 + prompt 10 + 100 moved from train) / test 500 / ood 163 (HumanEval+), plus plus_compatible (441 IDs: 55 train, 58 dev, 165 test, 163 ood) where the reference solution passes the MBPP+/HumanEval+ tests

Harness passes tests/test_harness.py: unbiased pass@k reported only for k <= n/2, bootstrap CIs over items, def-aware code extraction, rlimit sandbox, threads + fresh-subprocess verifier (safe after jax import) with measured throughput (4128 programs in 18.2 s on 30 workers = 226 programs/s)

Spine chosen by rule 3.1: Qwen3-1.7B passes scripts/week0_jax_smoke.py (Tunix NNX load, greedy generation, qwix LoRA forward/backward with the optimizer filtered to LoRAParam), with Qwen3-0.6B named in advance as the second choice
Dev gate measured (basic pass@8 = 65.6% [59.3, 71.8], inside the 10-70% gate) and the noise floor measured as the SD of test pass@1 across 3 scored sampling seeds (basic 0.17 pts, plus 0.66 pts)

SFT source named and built: the sftpool run on train (274 x 16) scored, and data/sft_pool_qwen3-1_7b.jsonl = 274 MBPP references + verified self-samples (basic and plus pass, finish_reason=stop, deduplicated, at most 4 per prompt)
deliverables: envs/jax/uv.lock and envs/torch/uv.lock committed
data/splits.json (frozen; test never changes) with plus_compatible
harness/ (build_data, prompts, verifier, _sandbox_runner, stats, score) and tests/test_harness.py green
scripts/gen_vllm.py, scripts/week0_overnight.sh, scripts/week0_report.py, scripts/week0_jax_smoke.py

learned: You can derive the unbiased pass@k estimator, compute it by hand for a small (n, c, k), explain why the plug-in estimate is biased low, and say why the report stops at k = n/2
You can separate the two kinds of uncertainty in an eval number, item sampling (bootstrap CI over items) and completion sampling (noise floor across seeds), and predict each from per-item pass rates
You can explain why a stricter verifier must agree with the original spec before you trust it, and why held-out sets are frozen as ID lists
You can debug an eval pipeline from status counts and error details, separating extraction bugs from model mistakes
You can explain why forking a process after JAX has initialized CUDA is unsafe while threads that launch fresh subprocesses are fine, and what the sandbox does not protect against
You can do the memory arithmetic for Qwen3-1.7B: bf16 weights, full-vocab logits at a given B and L, and KV cache per token
You can diagnose a recompile and a silent shell-script failure from their symptoms

questions.q: An item has n=16 samples and c=4 pass. Compute unbiased pass@8 and the plug-in estimate 1-(1-c/n)^8. Which is larger, why is the plug-in biased in that direction, and why does harness/stats.py report pass@k only for k <= n/2?
good_answer: Unbiased pass@k = 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k) = 1 - C(12,8)/C(16,8) = 1 - 495/12870 = 0.9615; the code uses the stable product form 1 - prod_{i=n-c+1..n}(1 - k/i) and returns 1 when n - c < k
Plug-in: 1 - 0.75^8 = 0.8999, about 6 pts lower

f(p) = 1-(1-p)^k is concave, so by Jensen E[f(p_hat)] <= f(E p_hat) = f(p): plugging in the sample rate is biased low. The combinatorial form is the exact probability that a uniformly random size-k subset of the n samples contains a pass, whose expectation over draws equals the true pass@k

As k approaches n the estimate collapses toward the indicator 1[c > 0], which has high variance per item; requiring n >= 2k (protocol 3.2.6) keeps many distinct subsets per item. That is why the gate used n=16 to report pass@8 directly instead of a pass@4 lower bound
pass@1 is always reported because it equals c/n
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then run pass_at_k(16, 4, 8) from harness/stats.py and compare with test_pass_at_k_matches_closed_form in tests/test_harness.py; Claude probes the Jensen argument

questions.q: The dev gate gave basic pass@8 = 65.6% [59.3, 71.8] and pass@1 = 49.8%. Interpret the gate result. Then predict the noise floor: the SD of test pass@1 across 3 sampling seeds with 500 items x 4 samples each. Give the formula, an upper bound, and a better estimate. How does it compare with the bootstrap CI half-width on the same run, and how far can you trust an SD from 3 seeds?
good_answer: Gate passes on the point estimate (10% <= 65.6% <= 70%), but the upper CI crosses 70%, so the model is near the top of the gate. Most of the headroom for SFT and RL is the ~16 pt gap between pass@1 and pass@8, which is sharpening rather than new capability

Per-seed variance from completion sampling with items fixed: Var = (1/N^2) * sum_i p_i(1-p_i)/n = mean(p(1-p))/(N*n) with N=500, n=4. Upper bound at p_i = 0.5: sqrt(0.25/2000) = 1.1 pts. Items are strongly bimodal (most always pass or always fail): pooling the 12 samples per item gives mean p(1-p) of about 0.035, so predicted SD = sqrt(0.035/2000) = 0.42 pts

Measured: basic 45.9 / 45.6 / 45.9 gives SD 0.17 pts (2x bar = 0.35 pts); plus on 165 items 55.9 / 55.8 / 57.0 gives 0.66 pts (bar 1.3 pts). Plus is noisier because it has fewer items (SD scales as 1/sqrt(N))

Bootstrap CI over items asks a different question (a different set of problems): between-item SD of per-item pass@1 is about 0.47, so SE = 0.47/sqrt(500) = 2.1 pts and half-width about 4.1 pts, matching the reported [41.8, 49.9]. That is 10-25x the noise floor, so for later comparisons the paired CI, not the 2x-noise-floor bar, is the binding criterion

3 seeds give 2 degrees of freedom: at 95%, s/sigma lies in [0.16, 1.92], so the true SD lies in about [0.52 s, 6.3 s], here roughly 0.09 to 1.1 pts. 0.17 is consistent with the 0.42 prediction. Treat it as an order of magnitude and re-measure when the sampler changes (week 3)
questions.verify: Write the prediction down first, then compute mean p(1-p) from the three runs/week0_noise_test_qwen3-1_7b_s*/scored.jsonl files with Claude and compare with the noise-floor lines in runs/week0_report_qwen3-1_7b.md; also confirm the seeds really differ (only 27 of 2000 completions are identical between s0 and s1)

questions.q: build_data.py keeps MBPP+ tests only where the MBPP reference solution passes them, dropping 101 items (100 MBPP + 1 HumanEval+), and freezes the survivors as splits.json["plus_compatible"]. Why not use every MBPP+ test? What would go wrong if this list were recomputed at score time instead of frozen? Why is the dev plus number (58 items) much less useful than dev basic, and why is test plus pass@1 (about 56%) higher than test basic (about 46%)?
good_answer: MBPP+ rewrote some specs (signatures, return types, names). A model that follows the MBPP prompt exactly would fail those tests, so the stricter verifier would measure disagreement with a changed spec, not correctness. Requiring the reference to pass is the minimal check that the tests match the task as prompted. HumanEval+ items whose canonical solution fails are removed entirely, because OOD items have no basic tests to fall back on

Frozen IDs make the held-out denominator immune to dataset revisions, verifier changes (timeouts, rlimits, pre-imports) and flaky tests; recomputing at score time lets the item set move between runs and breaks paired comparisons across weeks

MBPP+ covers only part of MBPP (378 items, of which 278 survive: 55 train, 58 dev, 165 test). With 58 items the dev plus pass@1 CI is about +/-11 pts ([42.5, 64.4] in the gate), so it cannot resolve small differences

The plus subset is not a random sample: it is built from the cleaner, sanitized MBPP subset, so it is easier. The 56% vs 46% gap is selection, not a stricter verifier being easier. To report the stricter-verifier gap, compare basic vs plus on the same 165 test IDs
questions.verify: Explain aloud; Claude asks you to point to the filtering lines in harness/build_data.py, count plus coverage per split from data/splits.json, and compute basic pass@1 restricted to the 165 plus-compatible test IDs

questions.q: Debug this symptom: a scored run shows many basic="error" rows with detail "NameError: name 'add' is not defined", yet the raw completion visibly contains a correct def add. What is the cause, what is the fix in harness/prompts.py, and which failure modes does the fix still leave? The current dev gate still shows 530 errors out of 3200 basic results, 174 of them NameError. How do you tell extraction bugs from genuine model mistakes, and what does that split look like here?
good_answer: Qwen3 often writes the solution block and then a trailing usage block (asserts or prints). Taking the last fenced block drops the def, so the test program calls an undefined name

Fix: choose the last fenced block that matches the def regex, else the last block, else the raw text; strip <think> blocks first; accept an unterminated final fence; prepend the HumanEval prompt when only a body is returned. Regression test: test_extract_code_skips_trailing_usage_block

Still broken: a helper in one block and the main function in a later block (only the last def block is kept); a last block that defines a test_ function instead of the solution; unfenced prose mixed with code

Triage: for each NameError, check whether the missing name is defined anywhere in the raw completion. Here 170 of 174 name a function the model never defined (it renamed the function the prompt's example test calls, e.g. mbpp/521 check_isosceles), and only 4 are extraction losses. TypeError (230, mostly wrong signatures) and IndexError point at the model misreading the spec; AssertionError counts as fail, not error
Because completions.jsonl is separate from scoring, an extractor change is fixed by re-scoring, not regenerating, and every baseline must be re-scored with the same extractor before comparison
questions.verify: Show the pytest in tests/test_harness.py, then with Claude group basic_detail in runs/week0_gate_dev_qwen3-1_7b/scored.jsonl and reproduce the 170 vs 4 split for NameErrors

questions.q: harness/verifier.py uses a ThreadPoolExecutor where each thread calls subprocess.run on a fresh `python -I -B _sandbox_runner.py`. Why is this safe to call from a process that already imported jax, when a fork-based multiprocessing pool is not? Name three things model-written code can still do despite the sandbox, and explain why the env sets OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 and PYTHONHASHSEED=0.
good_answer: fork copies the parent's address space, including the CUDA context and locks held by XLA's background threads at fork time; the child can deadlock or crash when it touches them. The parent threads only wait in subprocess.run (GIL released), and the child execs a new interpreter with -I (no user site, no cwd on sys.path) and a minimal env, so no jax state exists in it

The runner sets rlimits (RLIMIT_AS 4 GB, RLIMIT_CPU timeout+1, RLIMIT_FSIZE 16 MB, no core files) and a reliability guard that sets selected os/shutil/subprocess functions to None. It is not a security boundary: code can import posix and call posix.unlink, use os.execv or os.posix_spawn (not in the guard list) or ctypes, overwrite files by absolute path with open(path, 'w'), read anything the user can read (e.g. ~/.ssh), and open network sockets. Week 7 agents need a container or VM

Thread caps: each runner pre-imports numpy, whose OpenBLAS/OpenMP pools default to one thread per core; 30 concurrent children would oversubscribe the CPU, and per-thread buffers count against RLIMIT_AS, which can turn into spurious MemoryError or thread-creation failures recorded as error
PYTHONHASHSEED=0 fixes set and str-keyed hash order inside test programs, so the same code gets the same verdict on every re-score
Measured throughput: 226 programs/s on 30 workers, about 0.13 s per program per worker (mostly interpreter plus numpy startup), well under the 1 s/sample budget
questions.verify: Explain aloud; Claude probes follow-ups, then write a two-line program that deletes a file in a temp dir via posix.unlink, run it through run_program, and show that it returns pass

questions.q: Do the memory arithmetic for scripts/week0_jax_smoke.py with Qwen3-1.7B (28 layers, d=2048, 16 q heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, MLP 6144, vocab 151936, tied embeddings). Compute: bf16 weight bytes; one [B, L, V] logits tensor at B=2, L=512 in bf16 and fp32; KV cache per token and for cache_size=1024. Predict the logits term at B=8, L=1024. Why does the printed peak overstate the train-step footprint, and why does the script reload the model with RematConfig.DECODER for training instead of reusing the sampler's model?
good_answer: Per layer: attention 2*2048*2048 + 2*2048*1024 = 12.6M, MLP 3*2048*6144 = 37.7M, total 50.3M; x28 = 1.41B; embedding 151936*2048 = 311M (tied, counted once); total about 1.72B, so bf16 weights = 3.44 GB

Logits 2*512*151936 = 155.6M elements: 0.31 GB bf16, 0.62 GB fp32. The loss path holds several such tensors (bf16 logits, fp32 upcast, log_softmax output, fp32 grad softmax - onehot, its bf16 cast for the lm_head backward), so roughly 2-3 GB scaling with B*L. Remat'd layer boundaries are small by comparison ([2, 512, 2048] bf16 = 4 MB per layer)
KV cache per token = 2 (K, V) * 28 layers * 8 KV heads * 128 * 2 bytes = 112 KiB; 1024 tokens = 112 MiB (117 MB) per sequence

At B=8, L=1024 the logits are 8x larger: 1.25B elements = 5 GB per fp32 copy, about 15-20 GB for the loss path on top of 3.4 GB of weights, which OOMs on 24 GB. Hence small microbatches now and chunked log-softmax with scan + remat in week 3

peak_bytes_in_use is a process-lifetime high-water mark, so it includes the load and sampler phase; attribute memory with train_step.lower(...).compile().memory_analysis() or by measuring phases in separate processes. Remat trades memory for recompute in the backward pass, so inference gains nothing; in this Tunix version DECODER remat broke the KV-cache sampler, so the script deletes the sampler model and loads a remat copy for training
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the [lora], [optimizer] and [memory] lines in the saved smoke-test log; Claude checks each multiplication

questions.q: Suppose that in the smoke test step 0 of train_step is slow (compile, expected) but step 1 is also slow, and only step 2 is fast. What does that pattern mean, how do you find the exact cause, and what assertion would catch it permanently? Also: the smoke test's train_step closes over the module-level arrays positions and attn. What does that do to the compiled program, and when does it start to matter?
good_answer: Step 1 recompiled: the jit cache key (pytree structure plus shape, dtype, weak_type and sharding of each leaf, plus static args) differed between call 0 and call 1, so something step 0 returned is not identical in type to what was passed in

Typical causes: optimizer state or step count initialized with a weak-typed Python scalar or a different dtype than the update produces; init arrays uncommitted or with a different sharding than the step's outputs; a change in NNX graph structure or a Python attribute between calls

Diagnose with jax.config.update('jax_log_compiles', True) and jax_explain_cache_misses, which names the argument that changed; or dump jax.tree.map(lambda x: (x.shape, x.dtype, x.weak_type, x.sharding), nnx.state(...)) before and after step 0 and diff

Fix by making init match the step's outputs (explicit dtypes, device_put with the same sharding), or one documented warmup step; then assert that N steps after warmup trigger zero compiles (the week-3 zero-recompile assertion)

Closed-over jax arrays are baked into the HLO as constants: attn is [B, L, L] bool (0.5 MB at 2x512, 8 MB at 8x1024), so compile time and executable size grow with it, and any new shape needs a new trace anyway. In week 1 pass masks and positions as arguments
questions.verify: Re-run the smoke test with jax_log_compiles on, show Claude the compile log lines (one per step function on a clean run), then deliberately change the optimizer init dtype and show the extra compile and the cache-miss explanation

questions.q: Two infra failures from week 0. (a) An earlier week0_overnight.sh used `gen ... && score ...` under `set -euo pipefail`. Generation crashed for one seed, yet the script ran on and printed a report. Why? (b) vLLM crashed while compiling a sampling kernel because nvcc rejected the host gcc. Explain the cause, why gen_vllm.py sets VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER in os.environ before `from vllm import ...`, and what protocol consequence a sampler change has.
good_answer: Bash ignores errexit for any command in an && or || list except the last one; a failing gen on the left of && only makes the list return nonzero, so the script moves on. Errexit is also ignored inside a function called in such a context, in if/while conditions, and after !

Fix in the repo: run() executes gen and score as separate statements. score() itself ends in `python ... && echo`, which is fine: the function returns nonzero, and because score is called as a plain statement, set -e fires in the caller

Symptom to watch for: a run dir with completions.jsonl but no summary.json, and a report whose noise floor uses fewer seeds than intended (week0_report.py computes it from whatever seed summaries exist)

FlashInfer JIT-compiles sampling kernels with nvcc at runtime, and nvcc refuses host gcc versions newer than it supports (gcc > 14 here). VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 selects vLLM's built-in sampler. Setting it in os.environ before importing and constructing LLM guarantees both vllm's env config and the engine-core subprocess vLLM spawns see it; setdefault lets a user override it. The flake also uses mkShellNoCC so nix does not inject its own compiler

Different samplers use different RNG streams and numerics, so per-seed samples and speed change. Record the sampler and its version in meta (3.2.8) and re-measure the noise floor whenever it changes (3.2.3)
questions.verify: Reproduce (a) with `bash -c 'set -e; false && true; echo still running'` and show Claude; point to the os.environ.setdefault line in scripts/gen_vllm.py and the shellHook in flake.nix

weeks.exit_check: You are done with week 0 when pytest passes, every run dir (gate, 3 noise seeds, sftpool) has a summary.json, runs/week0_report_qwen3-1_7b.md shows the dev gate, the basic and plus noise floor from 3 seeds and the SFT pool size, results rows carry the 3.2.8 meta from a clean git SHA, and you can answer every question above without looking at the code.
pitfalls: Reporting a noise floor from fewer than 3 seeds because one step failed silently; check that every run dir has a summary.json

Comparing numbers scored with different extractors or verifier settings, or from a dirty tree whose SHA cannot reproduce them; re-score all baselines after any harness change and commit before headline runs
Reading peak_bytes_in_use as the train-step footprint when it is a process-lifetime high-water mark
Running vLLM and JAX on the GPU at the same time, or importing torch and jax in one process

weeks.title: SFT + LoRA
weeks.theme: Week 1 builds the first training loop and the masked log-prob function that DPO, KL and GRPO will reuse, and asks whether SFT on verified code helps without causing forgetting.

questions.q: Count the LoRA parameters for rank 16 on all 7 linear projections of Qwen3-1.7B (q: 2048->2048, k and v: 2048->1024, o: 2048->2048, gate and up: 2048->6144, down: 6144->2048, 28 layers). How much memory do LoRA params, grads and Adam state take in fp32? What would an unfiltered optimizer cost? Why is B initialized to zero, and how many params would attn-only LoRA have?
good_answer: Each adapted matrix adds r(d_in + d_out): q and o 16*4096 = 65,536 each; k and v 16*3072 = 49,152 each; gate, up and down 16*8192 = 131,072 each. Per layer 622,592; x28 = 17.43M, about 1% of 1.72B
fp32: params 70 MB, grads 70 MB, Adam m and v 139 MB, about 280 MB in total

Unfiltered: fp32 Adam m+v for 1.72B params = 13.8 GB, plus 3.4 GB of bf16 grads, plus 3.4 GB of weights, over 20 GB before activations, so OOM on 24 GB; and if it fit, you would be training the base model by accident

Delta W = (alpha/r) * A @ B with A random (he_uniform in qwix) and B = 0, so Delta W = 0 at step 0 and SFT starts exactly at the base model; with alpha = 2r (as in the smoke test) the scale is 2. Gradients still flow to B because dL/dB depends on A, not on B
Attn-only: 2*65,536 + 2*49,152 = 229,376 per layer, 6.42M total, so an attn-only vs all-linear ablation also changes capacity by 2.7x
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the [lora] trainable line and the [optimizer] state count printed by scripts/week0_jax_smoke.py

questions.q: Write (or point to) the train step and the test that proves only LoRA params train. What exactly does the test assert? What is the difference between nnx.Optimizer(..., wrt=nnx.LoRAParam) and argnums=nnx.DiffState(0, nnx.LoRAParam), and what goes wrong if only one of them is filtered? With batches padded to length buckets {256, 512, 768, 1024} and a fixed microbatch size, how many compiles do you expect over an epoch?
good_answer: nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adamw(lr), wrt=nnx.LoRAParam) creates optimizer state only for LoRA leaves; nnx.value_and_grad(loss_fn, argnums=nnx.DiffState(0, nnx.LoRAParam)) differentiates only LoRA leaves (names as in Flax 0.12; check the installed version)

If grads are unfiltered but the optimizer is filtered, you still compute and hold 1.72B grads (3.4 GB) every step; if the optimizer is unfiltered, you allocate 13.8 GB of Adam state and update base weights

Test asserts: OptState mu and nu leaves match the LoRA leaves one to one (plus the step counters); OptState elements = 2 * 17.43M at 4 bytes each; after one step on a nonzero loss, every nnx.Param that is not a LoRAParam is bit-identical (jnp.array_equal) while lora_b has changed
The model, optimizer, batch, loss mask and positions are nnx.jit arguments, never closed over; a closure bakes arrays into the HLO as constants and forces retracing when they change

Expect one compile per distinct (B, L) shape, so at most 4, plus possibly one extra at step 1 if the initial state types differ from the step's outputs; confirm with jax_log_compiles. Without buckets every new max length recompiles
questions.verify: Show the pytest passing, then run 20 steps over mixed buckets with jax_log_compiles on and show Claude the compile count

questions.q: Protocol 3.1 says LoRA params and Adam moments are fp32. Check what scripts/week0_jax_smoke.py actually creates: what dtype do qwix's LoRA params and optax.adamw's mu and nu have, and why? Use bf16 numbers to show what that does to training. If you then cast the LoRA params to fp32, what happens to the LoRA matmuls and the layer outputs, and how do you keep fp32 masters with bf16 compute? Finally, why is the merge W' = W + s*A@B done in fp32, and what check proves the merged checkpoint matches?
good_answer: qwix (providers/lora.py) takes lora_dtype from the base param, so LoRA A and B are bf16, and optax.adamw creates mu and nu in the param dtype, so they are bf16 too: the smoke test currently violates the rule, and a test asserting 4 bytes per OptState element would fail

bf16 has 8 significant bits (relative half-spacing 2^-8, about 0.39%). qwix's he_uniform A with fan_in 2048 has |a| up to sqrt(6/2048) = 0.054; for |a| >= 2^-5 = 0.031 the spacing is 2^-12 = 2.4e-4, so a ~1e-4 Adam step is under half a spacing and rounds away. B starts at 0, where spacing is tiny, so loss still falls early and hides the bug

Adam's second moment v <- 0.999 v + 0.001 g^2 changes by about 1e-3 relative per step, below bf16's 3.9e-3 half-spacing, so v stops tracking the gradients; the exponent range is fine, the precision is not

Fix: cast nnx.state(model, nnx.LoRAParam) to fp32 and nnx.update before building the optimizer. But jax.lax.dot_general(bf16, fp32) promotes to an fp32 result, so the LoRA delta and then base_out + delta become fp32: fp32 matmuls and doubled activation memory downstream. Cast A and B to bf16 inside the matmul (a wrapper around the LoRA call) so grads flow back to the fp32 masters, and assert each layer's output is bf16

Merge: if |s * DeltaW_ij| is under half a bf16 spacing of W_ij, adding in bf16 erases it; compute W + s*A@B in fp32 and cast once. Check per-token log-probs of the merged bf16 model vs base+adapter on 5 or more fixed sequences, reporting max abs difference and mean NLL difference (expect around 1e-2); week 4's RL reference test is the same check
questions.verify: Print jax.tree.map(lambda x: x.dtype, ...) for the LoRAParam and OptState of the smoke-test model, show Claude bf16 before your fix and fp32 after, plus the dtype of one decoder layer's output; point to the lora_dtype line in qwix/_src/providers/lora.py; then show the merged-vs-adapter parity output

questions.q: Write the core of the masked per-token log-prob function in a few lines, including how labels and mask are shifted. Then compute by hand: a completion of two code tokens and <|im_end|> whose targets get probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.8, followed by a pad position (masked) whose target gets 0.1. What is the masked mean NLL? Also predict the loss of a pretrained model on uniformly random token IDs, as in the week-0 smoke test.
good_answer: logits[:, :-1] predicts ids[:, 1:]; the mask is loss_mask[:, 1:], where loss_mask is 1 on assistant completion tokens including the <|im_end|> EOS and 0 on prompt tokens and pads

Upcast logits to fp32 before log_softmax; logp_t = logits_t[y_t] - logsumexp(logits_t), gathered with take_along_axis; return per-token logp times mask and reduce outside, so SFT can take a masked mean while DPO and GRPO take per-sequence sums

Hand value: (ln 2 + ln 4 + ln 1.25)/3 = ln 10 / 3 = 0.768. The pad contributes exactly 0 and is not in the denominator; dropping the EOS term would give 1.040 instead, which is how the test catches a missing EOS
Pytests: changing prompt-token labels leaves the loss unchanged; EOS is in the target; pads are excluded; parity vs HF PyTorch NLL from saved .npy files within about 1e-2 in bf16

Random IDs: a uniform predictor gives ln V = ln 151936 = 11.93; a pretrained model is confident and wrong on random text, so expect about 12 or more. The smoke test's unmasked .mean() over all positions is what this function replaces
questions.verify: Derive 0.768 on paper first, then show the pytest with the hand-computed case passing; Claude asks you to break the shift or drop EOS on purpose and predict which test fails

questions.q: Debug this symptom: after SFT, dev pass@1 is lower than base, finish_reason=length rises from 10/3200 to several hundred, and some completions start with an unexpected <think> block. List the likely causes in the data and mask pipeline, and the check that confirms each.
good_answer: EOS missing from the loss mask: the model never learns to emit <|im_end|>, so it runs to max_tokens (768). Check: decode the masked-in tokens of 3 examples and confirm the last one is <|im_end|>

Template mismatch: eval uses apply_chat_template(..., add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False), which ends the prompt with an empty <think>\n\n</think> block. If the SFT text was built differently (another template call, or without that block), train and eval prefixes differ. Check: build training ids from exactly the gen_vllm.py prompt call and diff the strings

Mask off by one at the prompt boundary: tokenizing the prompt string alone and the full string can give different tokens at the join. Check: build ids by concatenating prompt token IDs, completion token IDs and the EOS ID, or assert ids(prompt) is a prefix of ids(full) for every pool item

Pads in the loss, or pad id equal to EOS so EOS is masked by accident (Qwen3 pads with <|endoftext|>, ends turns with <|im_end|>). Check: count masked-in pad IDs, which must be 0, and that EOS positions have mask 1
Confirm the fix by re-scoring and comparing status_counts, finish_reason and mean length against the week-0 baseline, not only pass@1
questions.verify: Explain aloud; Claude probes follow-ups, then show the prefix assertion and the decoded masked-in tokens for 3 pool items

questions.q: Estimate SFT cost on the 4090. Take your actual pool size from runs/week0_report_qwen3-1_7b.md (expect several hundred to ~1000 examples of ~300-350 tokens; the measured mean completion is 219 tokens). Count FLOPs per token for LoRA training with a frozen base and decoder remat, then wall time per epoch at a realistic MFU. Then choose a microbatch size from the logits memory at L=512.
good_answer: Forward 2N per token with N = 1.72B (the tied lm_head matmul counts once; the embedding lookup is free); backward through activations 2N; no base weight grads (saves the usual 2N); remat recomputes the decoder forward, about +2N; LoRA terms and attention scores add a few percent. Total about 6N = 1.0e10 FLOP per token
At ~1000 examples x 350 tokens = 3.5e5 tokens per epoch: about 3.6e15 FLOP

4090 dense bf16 tensor peak with fp32 accumulate is about 165 TFLOP/s; at 30% MFU (~50 TFLOP/s) that is about 70 s per epoch, so compile time and eval generation dominate wall time, not training. MFU = achieved model FLOP/s divided by peak, counting 6N per token (not counting remat recompute as useful work if you report model-FLOP MFU)
Padding to a 512 bucket when the mean is 350 wastes about 30% of compute; buckets or packing recover it

Logits at L=512: B=2 is 0.62 GB per fp32 copy; B=8 is 2.5 GB per copy and about 8-10 GB for the loss path on top of 3.4 GB weights, so use microbatch 2-4 with gradient accumulation (e.g. optax.MultiSteps) to an effective batch of 16-32
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then time one epoch (excluding the first compiled step) and compare with the prediction; Claude asks you to explain any gap larger than 2x

questions.q: Before running it, predict how SFT on this pool (references plus the model's own verified samples) will change test pass@1, plus and OOD, and why. Then: you compare base vs SFT on 500 test items with per-item pass@1 from n=4 samples. Why is a paired bootstrap the right test, how wide do you expect it to be compared with the unpaired difference, why is McNemar wrong here, and what must hold before you call the gain real?
good_answer: Prediction: training on the model's own verified samples is rejection-sampling fine-tuning (expert iteration); it mostly moves pass@1 toward pass@k (sharpening) on items the model can already solve, so expect a modest pass@1 gain of a few points on test, a smaller or zero gain on OOD, and fewer spec errors only if the references teach naming and signatures. Write the numbers down

Per-item difference d_i = SFT_i - base_i over shared IDs; resample items with replacement and take the 2.5/97.5 percentiles of mean(d) (stats.paired_bootstrap). Use the same decoding config, chat template and extractor for both arms; pooling the three base noise seeds (n=12 per item) reduces base-side sampling noise

Width: one arm's half-width is about 4.1 pts (between-item SD 0.47, SE 2.1); an unpaired difference is about sqrt(2) x 4.1 = 5.8 pts. Paired, SD(mean d) = SE * sqrt(2(1 - rho)) with rho the per-item correlation between arms; at rho = 0.8 that is about +/-2.6 pts, so a 2-3 pt gain is near the resolution
McNemar needs one binary outcome per item per arm (e.g. greedy pass@1). Per-item rates averaged over 4 samples are not binary, so use the paired bootstrap or a Wilcoxon signed-rank test

A headline claim needs gain > 2x the noise floor (0.35 pts basic, 1.3 pts plus, so rarely binding), the paired CI excluding 0, and the same sign on every training seed. With one seed the third cannot be checked and training-seed variance is not in the CI, so label the result exploratory; the 3-seed re-run is in week 4. About 5 comparisons (basic, plus, OOD, general slice, ablation) is at the Holm threshold, so correct or label them exploratory
questions.verify: Commit the prediction before the run, then run paired_bootstrap on the base and SFT scored.jsonl files, report the measured rho, and explain the CI to Claude

questions.q: Design the forgetting check and the attn-only vs all-linear ablation so that neither result is confounded. How do you score the ~200-item multiple-choice general slice, which test applies there, what is the smallest drop you can detect, and how do you make the ablation a fair comparison?
good_answer: Freeze the slice by ID as a new splits.json key (check the license; test stays untouched); use the same chat template for base and SFT

Score by comparing the next-token log-probs of the option letters with the week-1 log-prob function and taking the argmax: deterministic, no sampling noise, and immune to format drift. Generating and parsing an answer would mix forgetting with the formatting changes that SFT on code causes
Each item is then one binary outcome per arm, so McNemar is valid here (unlike the sampled code metric), as is a paired bootstrap; only the discordant items carry information

Resolution: at 200 items and p about 0.5 a single proportion has a CI of about +/-7 pts; if SFT flips only a handful of answers the paired test is much tighter, but only drops of a few points are detectable, so state that limit next to the result

Ablation: attn-only rank 16 has 6.4M params vs 17.4M for all-linear, confounding placement with capacity. Match params (attn-only rank 43, since 17.43M / (28 * 14,336 per unit rank) = 43.4) or report both; keep data, steps, effective batch and seed identical, give each arm its own small lr sweep, and label it exploratory with one seed
questions.verify: Explain the design aloud before building it; Claude probes the confounds, then show the frozen slice IDs and the McNemar or paired-bootstrap output

weeks.exit_check: You are done with week 1 when the LoRA-only, log-prob and paired_bootstrap pytests pass with LoRA params and Adam moments confirmed fp32, the results table shows base vs SFT on test, plus, OOD and the general slice with paired CIs and the noise-floor bar applied (labeled exploratory), and the merged SFT export matches the adapter model on log-prob parity.
pitfalls: Unfiltered nnx.grad or nnx.Optimizer, which silently trains or stores state for all 1.72B params
Trusting qwix defaults: LoRA params and Adam moments come out bf16 and round small updates to zero, while a naive fp32 cast silently turns the LoRA matmuls and activations fp32
EOS left out of the loss mask, or a prompt mask that is off by one at the template boundary
Putting the jax log-prob code inside harness/, which must stay framework-neutral and never import jax

DPO loss (~15 lines) built on the week-1 masked log-prob function. Reference log-probs are precomputed once from the SFT model with the same template and masks, before training. A pytest checks that the step-0 loss equals log 2.

Three arms trained and evaluated on frozen test plus dev: SFT, SFT + chosen-only, and SFT + DPO (beta=0.1). Both trained arms start from the SFT adapter and use matched steps and LR schedule. Single seed, labeled exploratory.
Each arm logs verifier pass rate, mean completion length, the chosen-minus-rejected implicit-reward margin, and chosen and rejected log-prob trends over steps.

Results table for 3 arms: test pass@1 with 95% CI, paired bootstrap CI vs SFT and DPO vs chosen-only, mean length, final margin, chosen log-prob delta. Each row logs the 3.2.8 fields: git SHA, config hash, chat template, decoding config, sampler version, seed, allocator settings, accelerator_hours, cost_usd, per-item JSONL path

You can write the DPO gradient and explain its per-pair weight sigmoid(-u), including its value at step 0.
You can explain why DPO needs a chosen-only (SFT on winners) control before any gain can be credited to the contrastive signal.
You can read DPO training curves and spot a falling chosen log-prob, a margin that grows by pushing rejected down, and length drift.
You can build on-policy preference pairs from a programmatic verifier and work out which prompts carry signal.

questions.q: Start from max over pi of E_y~pi[r(x,y)] - beta * KL(pi(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x)). Derive the optimal policy, invert it to express r in terms of pi, plug that into Bradley-Terry, and write the DPO loss. Where does Z(x) go?
good_answer: Rewrite the objective as -beta * KL(pi || pi_ref * exp(r/beta) / Z(x)) + beta * log Z(x). KL >= 0 with equality only at the target, so pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) * exp(r(x,y)/beta) / Z(x), where Z(x) = sum_y pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta).
Inverting gives r(x,y) = beta * log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta * log Z(x).
Bradley-Terry: P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigmoid(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)). The beta * log Z(x) term is the same for both completions of one prompt, so it cancels. That only works because each pair shares x.
Loss = -log sigmoid(beta * [(log pi_theta(y_w|x) - log pi_ref(y_w|x)) - (log pi_theta(y_l|x) - log pi_ref(y_l|x))]), where each log pi(y|x) is summed over completion tokens only, EOS included.
questions.verify: Derive it on paper, then explain it aloud. Claude probes why Z cannot cancel across pairs with different prompts.

questions.q: Write the gradient of the DPO loss with respect to theta. What is the per-pair weight? What are the loss value and the weight at step 0 if the policy equals the reference?
good_answer: Let Delta = log pi_theta - log pi_ref for each completion and u = beta * (Delta_w - Delta_l). Then dL/du = -sigmoid(-u).
grad L = -beta * sigmoid(-u) * (grad log pi_theta(y_w|x) - grad log pi_theta(y_l|x)). pi_ref is a constant.

The weight sigmoid(-u) = sigmoid(r_hat_l - r_hat_w) is near 1 when the implicit reward ranks the pair wrongly. It decays to 0 as the margin grows, so pairs that are already ranked correctly stop contributing.
At step 0 the policy (SFT adapter) equals the reference, so u = 0, loss = log 2 ~= 0.6931, and every pair has weight 0.5.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then show the pytest that asserts step-0 loss ~= 0.6931 on a real batch.

questions.q: Write the DPO loss in JAX, given per-token policy log-probs [B, T] for chosen and rejected, completion masks [B, T], and cached per-sequence reference log-probs [B]. Also return the metrics you log.
good_answer: Sequence log-prob = sum over T of (logp * mask), computed in fp32 with the mask covering completion tokens plus EOS. No mean over length, because the derivation uses the full sequence log-prob.
u = beta * ((lp_w - ref_w) - (lp_l - ref_l)); loss = mean(-jax.nn.log_sigmoid(u)). Use log_sigmoid instead of log(sigmoid(.)) for numerical stability.
Reference values come from the cache and are constants, so no gradient flows through them (stop_gradient is optional but documents intent).
Metrics: mean u/beta (log-ratio margin), the implicit rewards beta*(lp - ref) for chosen and rejected, the accuracy mean(u > 0), and mean lp_w and lp_l.
questions.verify: Show the function and its pytests (log 2 at step 0, masked tokens contribute 0). Claude asks what changes if you average per token instead of summing.

questions.q: Your DPO run shows step-0 loss 0.58 instead of 0.693. List the likely causes in the order you would check them.
good_answer: The policy does not start from the SFT adapter (a fresh or zero-init LoRA, or base weights), so pi_theta differs from pi_ref.
Reference log-probs were precomputed on different inputs: another chat template or enable_thinking setting, different tokenization, or EOS included in one sum and not the other.
Mask mismatch: prompt or pad tokens are counted in one of the two log-prob sums.
Numerics: the reference was computed with bf16 logits and no fp32 upcast, or with a different LoRA scale (alpha/r) than the policy.
Diagnose by recomputing reference log-probs online for one batch at step 0 and diffing them per sequence against the cache. The diff should be ~0 up to bf16 noise.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the step-0 assertion and a one-batch diff of online vs cached reference log-probs in the repo.

questions.q: You draw 4 samples per prompt, and a prompt has pass probability p. What fraction of prompts gets skipped? Compute it for p = 0.1, 0.3 and 0.7, and say which MBPP train prompts DPO actually learns from.
good_answer: Skip probability = p^4 + (1-p)^4 (all pass or all fail). Over the train set, the skip fraction is the average of this over each prompt's p.
Signal comes only from prompts of intermediate difficulty for the SFT model. Very hard and very easy prompts contribute nothing.

The kept pairs are a biased sample of train, and MBPP train is small (~274 here). Log the skip fraction and the pass-rate distribution of kept prompts. If too few pairs survive, use 8 samples per prompt or form several pass/fail pairs per prompt.
questions.verify: Compute on paper, then compare with the logged skip fraction from the pair-building run.

questions.q: Why is SFT + chosen-only the right control for SFT + DPO? What result pattern would show the contrastive term adds nothing? Which test do you use for the comparison, and when would McNemar be valid instead?
good_answer: DPO's pairs bring new on-policy passing solutions that the verifier has checked. SFT on just those chosen samples (same data, steps and LR schedule, starting from the SFT adapter) separates the effect of extra verified data from the effect of pushing failures down.
If DPO and chosen-only both beat SFT, but the paired DPO-minus-chosen-only CI straddles 0, the gain comes from the data, not the preference signal.

For per-item pass rates estimated from several samples, use the paired bootstrap over shared item IDs (or Wilcoxon signed-rank). McNemar is only valid for one binary outcome per item, such as greedy pass@1.

Three comparisons stay under the ~5 Holm threshold. With one training seed the CI covers item and sampling noise but not seed variance, so the result is exploratory. A gain should also exceed 2x the week-0 noise floor. The 3-seed re-run happens on week-4 nights.
Report length per arm, because a pass-rate change that comes with a length change may be a format or truncation effect.
questions.verify: Explain aloud and point to the paired_bootstrap calls (harness/stats.py) behind the table. Claude proposes other result patterns and you interpret each one.

questions.q: You log a chosen log-prob that falls steadily during DPO, while the margin grows and test pass rate stays flat or rises slightly. Explain the mechanism, and why it is common for code pairs sampled from the same model.
good_answer: The loss depends only on Delta_w - Delta_l, so both log-probs can fall as long as the rejected one falls faster.

Chosen and rejected samples from the same SFT model share many tokens: signature, imports, common idioms. The rejected-side gradient pushes down those shared tokens in the chosen sequence too, through shared parameters.
Probability mass moves to sequences that are neither y_w nor y_l. That can leave greedy or low-temperature pass rate fine, or it can produce off-distribution outputs.
This is why the plan requires reporting the chosen log-prob trend. A common fix is adding an NLL term on chosen (as in RPO), which a chosen-only arm partly approximates.
questions.verify: Explain aloud and point to the chosen/rejected log-prob plot. Claude probes with a 2-token toy example where the two sequences share their first token.

questions.q: You used beta = 0.1. Predict how training changes at beta = 0.01 and at beta = 1.0: how far the policy drifts from the reference before the loss saturates, and how much the gradient scale actually matters under Adam. Why do you log the margin both as beta-scaled reward and as a raw log-ratio?
good_answer: The sigmoid saturates once beta * (log-ratio margin) is a few units. Small beta needs a much larger log-ratio gap, so the policy drifts further from pi_ref (a weaker KL constraint). Large beta saturates after a small change and keeps the policy close to the reference.
The explicit beta factor in the gradient is mostly normalized away by Adam. The behavioral effect of beta comes through where the weight sigmoid(-u) decays, not through the step size.

The implicit reward is r_hat = beta * log(pi_theta/pi_ref). The beta-scaled margin is comparable to the loss, and margin/beta is the raw log-ratio gap, which measures drift and is comparable across beta values.
Small beta raises the risk of length drift and a collapsing chosen log-prob, so check length and chosen log-prob before trusting a pass-rate gain.
questions.verify: Explain aloud. Claude asks you to predict the curves of a short beta=0.01 run, and you compare against it if you run one overnight.

questions.q: Fill in scorecard row 1 (post-training) from your weeks 0-2 evidence. For each of the 7 criteria, what is the score, its weight and the linked evidence? What happens to an unlinked score? What would Surprise >= 4 have to look like from your DPO vs chosen-only results, and why does it matter that you wrote the prediction down before the run?
good_answer: Score each criterion 1-5. Weights are Surprise 3, iteration speed 2, follow-up feasibility 2, enjoyment 2, relevance 2, JAX/TPU leverage 1, public signal 1, for a maximum weighted total of 65. Each score links to a plot or table in the repo, and an unlinked score counts as 1
Iteration speed and feasibility come from measured wall-clock (for example, how long one DPO arm took from launch to scored row) and sized next experiments, not from impressions

Surprise >= 4 means a result that contradicts an expectation you wrote down before the run, stated as a hypothesis you could test. One example: DPO not beating chosen-only, which would mean the gain comes from the extra verified data, not the preference signal. A prediction written before the run is what makes the surprise checkable rather than read back into the results
This row feeds the week-10 top-2 selection and the week-13 rule that the chosen area needs a Surprise >= 4 row from your own data, so weak evidence now carries forward
questions.verify: Show the committed scorecard row with its links; Claude opens each link, checks that it supports the score, and asks for the pre-run prediction behind the Surprise score

weeks.exit_check: You are done with this week when the three-arm table with paired CIs, length, margin and chosen log-prob trend is committed with per-item JSONL paths and the 3.2.8 fields, the step-0 log 2 test passes, scorecard row 1 is filled with linked evidence, and you can derive DPO and its gradient on a blank page.
pitfalls: Summing log-probs over prompt tokens or padding, or averaging per token. This changes the implicit reward and breaks the step-0 log 2 check.
Starting DPO from base or a fresh adapter while the reference is the SFT model, or computing reference log-probs with a different chat template or thinking setting.
Claiming a DPO win without the chosen-only control, while ignoring a length change, or from one seed without the exploratory label.
Materializing full fp32 logits for chosen and rejected at long length and running out of memory (microbatch instead), or quietly computing the loss in bf16.

You can compute memory for weights, LoRA + Adam, KV cache, activations and logits for Qwen3-1.7B from config.json, and predict whether a batch fits on 24 GB.

questions.q: From the Qwen3-1.7B config.json, compute bf16 KV-cache bytes per token. How many GB do 256 sequences x 768 tokens take, and 64 x 768? Does the 256-sequence batch fit on a 4090 next to the weights? Why doesn't the plan's Qwen2.5 number carry over?
good_answer: Config: 28 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128. Per token: 28 x 8 x 128 x 2 (K and V) x 2 bytes = 114,688 B ~= 112 KB.
256 x 768 = 196,608 tokens, about 22.5 GB. 64 x 768 = 49,152 tokens, about 5.6 GB.

Weights: hidden 2048, intermediate 6144, about 50.3M params per layer x 28 = 1.41B, plus a 311M tied embedding, about 1.72B x 2 B ~= 3.44 GB. So 256 x 768 does not fit in 24 GB, and 64-96 sequences at 768 is the realistic range.

Qwen2.5-1.5B has 2 KV heads (~28.7 KB/token), while Qwen3-1.7B has 8, so the cache is 4x larger. Qwen3-0.6B also has 28 layers x 8 KV heads x 128, so the fallback model has the same KV cost per token.
questions.verify: Compute on paper, then compare with the cache array's nbytes and peak_bytes_in_use after prefill.

questions.q: Why is materializing [B, T, V] logits impossible at RL scale? Why does lax.scan over sequence chunks still not save memory unless the body is wrapped in jax.checkpoint? Give numbers for 256 x 768 with V = 151,936.
good_answer: In reverse-mode AD, scan stacks each iteration's residuals for the backward pass. Without remat it stores every chunk's logits (or their softmax), so total memory matches the full tensor.

With jax.checkpoint (or nnx.remat) on the chunk body, only the chunk inputs (hidden states [B, chunk, d], ~0.8 GB bf16 in total for 256 x 768 x 2048) are saved. Logits are recomputed in the backward pass, so peak memory is about one chunk's fp32 logits.
Per chunk: project with the tied embedding, upcast to fp32, take logsumexp, and gather the target logit. The output is [B, T] log-probs.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the memory test (compile().memory_analysis() or peak bytes) for the remat and no-remat variants.

questions.q: Two symptoms: (a) your fp32 JAX logits differ from HF fp32 by ~3e-3 max abs, uniformly across positions; (b) in bf16, greedy decode diverges from HF on 30% of prompts. For each, what do you check before touching model code, and how does the acceptance criterion handle it?
good_answer: (a) Matmul precision. On Ada, JAX may use TF32 for fp32 matmuls (10-bit mantissa). Set jax_default_matmul_precision to 'highest' before tracing, and turn off TF32 in torch (allow_tf32 False or set_float32_matmul_precision('highest'); verify for your versions). Small, uniform error points to precision, not to RoPE or mask bugs, which grow with position or appear at pads.
If (a) persists at 'highest', diff per-layer hidden states to find the first layer that diverges.

(b) is expected. bf16 rounding flips near-tied argmaxes, and after one flip the sequences differ completely. Greedy identity is therefore tested only in fp32, and a fp32 divergence counts as a bug only if the top-2 logit gap at the first divergence exceeds ~1e-3.
bf16 acceptance is top-1 agreement of at least 99% on teacher-forced positions plus a log-prob tolerance, which compares the same token IDs and so avoids the divergence cascade.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the parity report with fp32 numbers before and after the precision fix, and the bf16 top-1 rate.

questions.q: Write the Qwen3 parity checklist you verified against config.json and the HF modeling code. For each item, name the symptom you would expect if you got it wrong.
good_answer: QK-norm: RMSNorm over head_dim on q and k per head, after projection and before RoPE. Omitting it or applying it after RoPE gives large errors from layer 0.
attention_bias=false (no QKV bias, unlike Qwen2.5). tie_word_embeddings=true, so lm_head = embed^T and the loader must not expect lm_head.weight. Unlike Gemma, there is no sqrt(d) embedding scale.
GQA with 16 query heads and 8 KV heads: KV head j serves query heads 2j and 2j+1 (repeat_kv order). The wrong order mixes heads and breaks parity from layer 0.
rope_theta 1e6 with HF's rotate_half (split-halves) convention, not interleaved. The wrong theta or convention gives errors that grow with position.
rms_norm_eps 1e-6 with the variance computed in fp32, a final norm before lm_head, and the MLP down(silu(gate(x)) * up(x)) with intermediate 6144. Swapping gate and up produces garbage.
questions.verify: Explain aloud while pointing at the code and the config. Claude names a symptom and you name the bug.

questions.q: Batch-1 generation matches HF greedy exactly, but in a left-padded batch the shortest prompts produce garbage after a few tokens, and sometimes the whole batch goes NaN. Name the likely bugs in prefill and decode.
good_answer: Key padding mask missing in decode, or applied only in prefill, so real tokens attend to pad slots in the cache.

Position IDs inconsistent between prefill and decode. Prefill uses cumsum(mask) - 1 per row, while decode uses the shared cache index, so for rows with more padding the relative position between prompt and new tokens is off by the pad count. A constant per-row offset used consistently is harmless under RoPE.
Cache write index: with left padding every row writes at the same slot (prompt bucket length + step), and the mask must include that slot. Mixing per-row and shared indices corrupts short rows.

NaN: K/V computed at pad positions can be NaN or inf (for example from a -inf mask producing fully masked pad query rows in prefill). An additive mask does not remove a NaN score. Use a large finite negative or jnp.where on the scores, and zero out pad K/V.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the test that compares each batched row against its own batch-1 run, including one prompt that is mostly padding.

questions.q: jax_log_compiles shows a new compilation at every decode step. List three causes and the fix for each. How do you turn 'zero recompiles after warmup' into an assertion?
good_answer: A Python for-loop that grows the cache or sequence shape each step: use a preallocated cache with fixed max_len, write with dynamic_update_slice at a traced index, and run the loop in lax.while_loop.
The step index or another per-step value passed as a static argument (static_argnums or a Python value in the hash): make it a traced jnp scalar.

The jitted function is recreated each step (jax.jit or nnx.jit of a fresh lambda or closure inside the loop): build it once and pass params as arguments via nnx.split, with nnx.merge inside a plain jax.jit. Closing over params under a jit built once does not recompile, but it bakes stale constants into the executable.

Assertion: warm up every bucket, then count compile events (a logging handler on jax_log_compiles or a jax.monitoring listener; verify the API) over N more calls, including a LoRA scale toggle, and assert the count is unchanged.
questions.verify: Show the pytest that asserts zero recompiles, then rerun it with a deliberate static step argument to watch it fail.

questions.q: State the sampler log-prob contract RL needs. Why must RL rollouts use top-p = 1 with top-k off, and what residual mismatch do you expect in bf16?
good_answer: For each sampled token the sampler returns log_softmax(logits / T)[token] over the full, untruncated vocab. The trainer computes the same quantity teacher-forced on the same token IDs, with the same T, template and masks. Tokens after EOS/done are masked on both sides.

With top-k or top-p, sampling happens from a distribution renormalized over a subset. The behavior policy then differs from the trainer's pi, so the importance ratio pi_theta/pi_old is biased even with zero updates.
Acceptance: mean abs difference of about 1e-2 or less in bf16 between sampler and teacher-forced log-probs, at T=1 and T=0.7.

The residual comes from different kernels and accumulation order (incremental decode with a cache vs a full forward). It is the numerical floor below which deviations of the ratio from 1 are meaningless, and you log it for week 4.
questions.verify: Show the test comparing teacher-forced and sampler log-probs, with its measured mean abs diff at both temperatures.

questions.q: Design the Orbax resume test. What must be in the checkpoint, and what exact comparison proves resume is correct?
good_answer: Save the LoRA params (fp32), the optimizer state (Adam m, v and count), the step, the PRNG key (or the base seed, used with fold_in(step)), the data-order state, and the config hash. Frozen base weights are not saved.
Run A: 2N steps uninterrupted. Run B: N steps, kill the process, restore, then N more steps with the same data order.

Compare final LoRA params and optimizer state, plus per-step losses after the restore point. Require bitwise equality if you enable deterministic GPU ops (XLA_FLAGS --xla_gpu_deterministic_ops, verify), otherwise allclose at a stated tolerance.

Common failures: the optimizer count is not restored (wrong LR schedule and bias correction), the PRNG restarts from the initial key, the data iterator restarts at epoch 0, or a checkpoint is half-written when the kill lands.
questions.verify: Show the pytest and run it. Claude asks what fails, and how it shows up in the loss curve, if you drop the Adam count.

questions.q: Implement the two-level paired bootstrap for arm A vs arm B with 3 training seeds each. Write the resampling loop, and explain why resampling only items understates the CI.
good_answer: Each draw: resample seeds with replacement within A and within B independently (3 from 3 each), resample the shared item IDs with replacement once, and use the same item draw for both arms.
Statistic: the mean over resampled items of (mean over A's resampled seeds of the item score) - (mean over B's resampled seeds of the item score). The CI is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
Item-only resampling treats one training run as fixed and ignores training-seed variance, which is often comparable to the item effect for DPO and RL.

With 3 seeds, seed resampling is coarse (only a few distinct multisets), so also report the per-seed paired differences. A headline claim requires the same sign on every seed and a gain above 2x the noise floor.
Pytest: with zero seed variance the result matches the single-level paired_bootstrap, and with injected seed variance the CI gets wider.
questions.verify: Show the function and its pytest in harness/stats.py. Claude gives a synthetic case with high seed variance and you predict the CI width before running it.

questions.q: LoRA initializes B = 0 and A randomly. Derive the loss gradients with respect to A and B at step 0. Which one moves first, and what does this mean for the scale-0 reference test?
good_answer: Output h = W x + s * B A x with s = alpha / r. With g = dL/dh: dL/dB = s * g (A x)^T and dL/dA = s * B^T g x^T.
At step 0 B = 0, so dL/dA = 0 and only B gets a gradient. A starts receiving gradient after B's first update.
At init the LoRA model equals the base exactly, so a fresh RL adapter on the merged-SFT base starts equal to the reference policy.

Scale-0 test: with s passed as a traced 0.0, the output equals W x for any A and B. Reference log-probs on the merged-SFT base must then equal the SFT model's (base + unmerged SFT adapter) log-probs up to the bf16 rounding from the fp32 merge.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then show the merged == unmerged and scale-0 tests.

questions.q: You switch from vLLM to your own sampler and the noise-floor SD across 3 sampling seeds drops to nearly 0. Is that good news? What do you check?
good_answer: Almost certainly a PRNG bug: the same key reused across seeds, decode steps or batch rows, which makes samples identical or correlated.
Correct pattern: key = fold_in(base_key, seed), then fold_in(step) or a split per decode step, and one categorical draw over [B, V] (or per-row keys) so rows differ.
Check that samples for the same item differ across seeds and across rows with duplicated prompts, and that per-item pass rates are not all 0 or 1.
Confirm the temperature is actually applied (no greedy argmax path at T > 0), then re-measure. The noise floor has to be re-measured anyway because the sampler changed.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show a test that two seeds, and two duplicated rows, produce different tokens at T=1.

weeks.exit_check: You are done with this week when the five gates (parity report, sampler MVP with the teacher-forced log-prob test, LoRA tests, chunked log-prob memory test, Orbax resume test) and the two-level bootstrap tests pass in pytest on the 4090, the OOD split is frozen, and the memory budget and noise-floor v2 row are committed. Unfinished polish is logged for week 4 Mon-Tue AM.
pitfalls: Running parity tests at the default matmul precision (TF32), which produces ~1e-3 errors that hide or fake real bugs, or demanding bf16 greedy identity.
Copying the plan's Qwen2.5/Gemma memory numbers: Qwen3-1.7B has 8 KV heads and 3.44 GB of weights, so the cache is 4x larger and 256 x 768 does not fit.
Closing over params or re-creating the jitted function inside a loop, or using a Python-attribute LoRA scale, which bakes stale constants into the executable or retraces on toggle.
Scan without remat in the chunked log-prob, a NaN from a -inf mask poisoning padded batches, or polishing top-k/top-p before the MVP works on Wednesday.

weeks.title: RL foundations to LLM pipeline
weeks.theme: Before spending GPU nights on Qwen3-1.7B RL, you check on a toy problem that your gradient estimators behave as theory says, test the GRPO/RLOO/KL math by hand, and build a single-process sample-verify-train loop that fits in 24 GB and is fast enough to pass the throughput gate.
goals: Toy NNX transformer (~1M params) trained on a verifiable digit task (reverse/sort/sum) with 16-32 seeds in one vmapped program, with reward and gradient-variance curves and seed bands for no-baseline, leave-one-out and LOO + KL to reference.

GRPO advantage (with a no-std flag), RLOO advantage, a per-token clipped surrogate and the pre-registered KL placement ((a) k1 in the reward with no gradient, or (b) k3 as a loss) implemented. Tests use hand-computed values on 2 groups x 3 samples, including a zero-variance group (zero advantage, no NaN), plus a Monte Carlo KL-gradient test on a small categorical policy.

A pre-registered loop choice (default: (a) strictly on-policy) built as one process: sample, then CPU verification overlapped with reference log-probs, then microbatched gradient accumulation. The KV cache is freed before training, frozen base weights are not donated and LoRA + optimizer state are. It runs sample-train-sample twice with no 'Array has been deleted' and passes a memory test at the full week-5 config (32 prompts x 8, 512 new tokens) with headroom.
A 50-step smoke run on MBPP train prompts that logs the sampler-vs-trainer log-prob mismatch, with zero recompiles after warmup.

Throughput gate at 256 x 512: your tokens/s vs one vLLM reference number (separate process, different time, preallocation on). Pass if within 4x of vLLM or if the measured step time fits 300 steps in ~10 h. The measured number goes into the week 5-6 compute table either way. If it misses, the profiling plan takes week 5 Mon-Tue.
On nights, re-run the weeks 1-2 headline (base vs SFT vs DPO) on your own stack with 3 seeds, reported with the two-level paired bootstrap, per-seed signs and the noise-floor comparison.
deliverables: Toy RL plot: reward and log gradient variance vs step for each variant, mean plus per-seed band (16-32 seeds).
Tested loss module (GRPO/RLOO advantages, clipped surrogate, k1/k3 diagnostics, chosen KL placement, token aggregation) with passing pytests, including the categorical KL-gradient test.

Pre-registration note committed before the smoke run: loop (a) or (b), KL placement and beta, loss aggregation (per-sequence mean vs token sum over a constant), std normalization on or off and ddof, group size, rollout decoding (T, top-p=1, top-k off), compute plan.
Pipeline pytests: two sample-train cycles without deleted arrays, base weights unchanged after training, accumulated gradient matches full batch, week-5-config memory bound, zero-recompile assertion.
Smoke-run log (50 steps): reward, zero-variance fraction, k1, k3, entropy, clip fraction, mismatch distribution, tokens/s, step time split into sample/reference/train.
Throughput gate result (pass/fail, your tokens/s vs vLLM, measured step time) written into the week 5-6 compute table, plus a profiling plan if it failed.
Weeks 1-2 table with 3 seeds and two-level paired CIs. Optional GPU dry-run log (launch.sh, 20 RL steps, SIGKILL, resume, upload, delete) if not deferred to week 5 Mon.
learned: You can explain why a baseline that does not depend on the sampled action leaves the policy gradient unbiased, and show numerically on the toy task how much variance leave-one-out removes.
You can compute GRPO (both std conventions) and RLOO advantages by hand for a binary-reward group, and say exactly what an all-pass or all-fail group must produce.

You can derive why k1 used directly as a loss on on-policy samples has zero expected gradient, why k1 in the reward gives the true KL(pi||pi_ref) gradient, and which KL's gradient k3 used as a loss actually follows.

You can do the memory arithmetic for Qwen3-1.7B rollouts and training on a 24 GB 4090 (weights, LoRA + Adam, KV cache with 8 KV heads, logits chunk) and pick sampler sub-batch and microbatch sizes from it.

You can split NNX state into frozen and donated parts so the sampler, reference and trainer share base weights without copies or deleted-array errors, and use the merged-SFT base with RL-adapter scale 0 as the reference.
You can write gradient accumulation whose loss and gradient match the full batch under the pre-registered token normalization.
You can estimate step time from training FLOPs and the decode bandwidth roofline, and judge whether 300 steps fit in one night.
You can run a seed-fanout comparison with vmap and correct per-seed PRNG handling, and report a seeded comparison with the two-level paired bootstrap protocol.

questions.q: In the toy task you compare no-baseline, a group-mean baseline that includes the sample itself, and leave-one-out. Show that leave-one-out keeps the REINFORCE gradient unbiased, say what the include-self mean baseline does to the gradient for group size G, and say what dividing by the group std changes.
good_answer: E_{a~pi}[grad log pi(a)] = sum_a grad pi(a) = grad 1 = 0, so any baseline b that is independent of sample i gives E[(r_i - b) grad log pi(a_i)] = E[r_i grad log pi(a_i)].
The LOO baseline b_i is the mean of the other G-1 rewards, which are independent of a_i given the prompt, so it is unbiased.

The include-self mean depends on a_i, so the argument does not apply directly. But r_i - mean_all = ((G-1)/G)(r_i - mean_{-i}), so it is exactly LOO scaled by (G-1)/G. The direction is unbiased, and the gradient shrinks by that factor (0.875 at G=8), which acts like a smaller LR.

Dividing by the group std (which depends on every sample, a_i included) is not a constant rescale. It reweights prompts by 1/std, upweighting near-all-pass or near-all-fail prompts, so the gradient is no longer an unbiased estimate of the plain objective's gradient.
Variance falls because the baseline removes the shared reward offset. The toy plot should show lower gradient variance for LOO than for no-baseline at matched step.
questions.verify: Derive it on paper, then explain it aloud. Claude probes the include-self and std cases and asks you to point to the toy-RL variance plot.

questions.q: A group of G=8 MBPP rollouts has 3 passes (reward 1) and 5 fails (reward 0). Give the GRPO advantages with population std, then with ddof=1 std, then the RLOO advantages, then the no-std advantages. What must your code return for an all-fail group, and why can it NaN?
good_answer: With ddof=1, std = 0.518 (torch.std's default), so pass is 1.21 and fail is -0.72. The convention must be fixed and written in the pre-registration.
RLOO: pass 1 - 2/7 = 0.714, fail 0 - 3/7 = -0.429. Equivalently (G/(G-1))(r - mean).
No-std flag (Dr. GRPO style): r - mean = 0.625 and -0.375.

For an all-fail or all-pass group, r - mean = 0, so the advantage must be exactly 0. (r-mean)/std is 0/0 = NaN unless you add eps or use jnp.where(std > 0, ..., 0). The test asserts exact zeros and no NaN, and also that the gradient through the loss is finite.
questions.verify: Compute it on paper, then show the pytest with the 2 groups x 3 samples case and run it.

questions.q: Derive the gradient you get from using k1 = log(pi/pi_ref) directly as a loss on samples from pi, then from putting beta*k1 into the reward with no gradient, then from using k3 = (pi_ref/pi) - 1 - log(pi_ref/pi) as a loss. Which KL does each one actually push down?
good_answer: k1 as a loss: no gradient flows through sampling, so grad k1 = grad log pi, and E_pi[grad log pi] = 0. The expected gradient is zero, so it only adds noise.
k1 in the reward (option a): the gradient is E_pi[log(pi/pi_ref) grad log pi], which is exactly grad KL(pi||pi_ref), because the extra term E_pi[grad log pi] vanishes.

k3 as a loss: grad k3 = (1 - pi_ref/pi) grad log pi. Its expectation under pi is -sum_a pi_ref(a) grad log pi(a) = grad KL(pi_ref||pi), the opposite KL direction from the one k3 estimates. That is the bias.
As a value estimator, E_pi[k3] = KL(pi||pi_ref) with k3 >= 0 and low variance, so it is logged as a diagnostic either way.

The categorical test computes the Monte Carlo mean of each implementation's gradient over many samples, compares it with the exact grad KL(pi||pi_ref), and shows that only option (a) matches within tolerance.
questions.verify: Derive it on paper, then show the categorical-policy KL-gradient pytest and its tolerance. Claude asks you to predict which assertion fails for k1-as-loss and for k3.

questions.q: Do the memory budget for the week-5 config on Qwen3-1.7B (28 layers, hidden 2048, MLP 6144, 16 Q heads and 8 KV heads of dim 128, vocab 151936 tied, ~1.72B params) on a 24 GB 4090: weights, LoRA r=16 on all linear layers plus Adam, KV cache for 256 sequences x 768 tokens, and fp32 logits for a 16-sequence microbatch. What do you change so it fits?
good_answer: Weights: 1.72B x 2 bytes = ~3.4 GB in bf16. They are never donated and are shared by the sampler, reference and trainer.

LoRA r=16 per layer: q,o r*(2048+2048) each, k,v r*(2048+1024) each, gate,up,down r*(2048+6144) each, so 16 x 38,912 = ~0.62M. Times 28 = ~17.4M params. fp32 param + grad + 2 Adam moments = 16 B each, ~280 MB.

KV per token: 28 x 8 x 128 x 2 (K,V) x 2 bytes = 114,688 B = ~112 KB. That is 4x the plan's Qwen2.5 figure (2 KV heads). 256 x 768 = 196,608 tokens gives ~22.5 GB, which does not fit beside the weights.
So the sampler runs serial sub-batches (64 seqs = ~5.6 GB, 128 = ~11.3 GB) and frees the cache before the train phase.

Logits: 16 x 768 x 151936 x 4 B = ~7.5 GB in fp32 before the backward, so chunked log-probs under scan + remat are required (a 128-token chunk is ~1.2 GB) and the microbatch is sized against the remaining activation memory.
questions.verify: Derive it on paper, then compare it with compile().memory_analysis() output from your memory test. Claude checks each line of the arithmetic.

questions.q: Throughput gate: you need 300 steps in one ~10 h night. Estimate the train plus reference compute per step for 256 x 768 tokens on Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA and remat, then the minimum sampling tokens/s you need. Is decode compute-bound or bandwidth-bound at batch 64?
good_answer: Budget: 10 h / 300 = 120 s per step.

Forward = 2N = ~3.4 GFLOP/token (N includes the tied LM-head matmul, and attention FLOPs are small at 768 tokens). Training with a frozen base is forward 2N + activation-grad backward 2N + remat recompute 2N = ~6N, since LoRA weight grads are negligible. 196,608 tokens x 6N = ~2.0e15 FLOP, and the reference forward adds ~0.7e15.
At ~40% of the 4090's ~165 dense bf16 TFLOPS (fp32 accumulate) = ~66 TFLOPS, that is ~40 s. That leaves ~80 s to generate 256 x 512 = 131k tokens, so you need about 1.6-1.7k tok/s.

Decode at batch 64 reads ~3.4 GB of weights plus ~64 x 500 x 112 KB = ~3.6 GB of KV per step. At ~1 TB/s that is ~7 ms, or ~9k tok/s ideal. Compute is only 2N x 64 = ~0.2 TFLOP per step (~1-2 ms), so decode is bandwidth-bound and a bigger sub-batch raises throughput until KV memory limits it.

Write the measured number into the compute table, not this estimate. Gaps from the roofline come from the sub-batches all running to 512 without early exit, padding, recompiles and small-kernel launch overhead.
questions.verify: Derive it on paper, then compare it with the smoke-run tokens/s and step-time logs. Claude asks where the gap from the roofline comes from, and you point to a jax.profiler trace.

questions.q: Your loop runs one sample-verify-train cycle fine, but the second call to the sampler raises 'Array has been deleted'. What is the mechanism, and how should the state be split?
good_answer: donate_argnums lets XLA reuse the input buffers for the outputs, so after the call the donated Python arrays are invalid.
If the train step donates the whole model state, the frozen base weights that the sampler and reference still hold get deleted.

Fix: nnx.split into frozen base params (a non-donated argument shared by sampler, reference and trainer) and trainable LoRA + optimizer state (donated). The returned new state replaces the old references everywhere, the sampler's included.
Test: run sample, train, sample, train in a pytest and assert no exception, that base weights are unchanged (same values, ideally the same unsafe_buffer_pointer), and that the LoRA params did change.
questions.verify: Show the pytest that runs the cycle twice and point to the donate_argnums line in the train step.

questions.q: With gradient accumulation over 16 microbatches of 16 sequences, your accumulated gradient differs from the full-batch gradient on the same 256 sequences by much more than float noise. The loss is meant to be a token-level mean. What is the likely bug?
good_answer: Each microbatch takes a mean over its own tokens, then the microbatch means are averaged. When completion lengths differ, this weights tokens unequally compared with one mean over all tokens.
Fix: accumulate per-microbatch sums of masked token losses and divide by the global token count (or the pre-registered constant), computed before the scan.

If the pre-registered aggregation is GRPO-style (mean per sequence, then mean over sequences), divide each sequence by its own length and the total by the global number of sequences, not per microbatch.
For Dr. GRPO token-sum over a fixed constant (e.g. G x max_len), every microbatch divides by the same constant, so plain summation is already exact.
Test: full batch vs accumulated on a model small enough to fit both, in fp32, asserting closeness at ~1e-5.
questions.verify: Explain it aloud, then show the accumulation-equivalence pytest. Claude asks how the answer changes for each aggregation choice.

questions.q: With a strictly on-policy loop and mu=1, you compute pi_old with the trainer as stop_gradient of the current log-probs. What are the ratio, the clip fraction and the gradient? What changes if pi_old comes from the sampler's returned log-probs instead?
good_answer: rho = exp(logpi - stop_grad(logpi)) = 1 exactly, so min(rho A, clip(rho) A) = A, the clip fraction is 0, and the gradient is A grad log pi: plain REINFORCE with a baseline.

With sampler log-probs, rho = exp(logpi_trainer - logpi_sampler) reflects numerical mismatch (bf16, different kernels, KV-cache decode vs full forward). Your week-3 baseline is mean abs ~1e-2 per token.
That mismatch rarely crosses a 0.2 clip boundary, but rare low-probability tokens can, so log the clip fraction and the tails of the mismatch distribution, not only its mean.
Any top-p/top-k or temperature difference between sampler and trainer biases rho. RL rollouts must use the same T as the trainer's log_softmax(logits/T), with top-p=1 and top-k off.
questions.verify: Explain it aloud. Claude probes with a case of T=0.7 in the sampler and T=1 in the trainer and asks for the expected sign of the mismatch on sampled tokens.

questions.q: You vmap the toy transformer over 32 seeds and all 32 reward curves come out identical. Then, after fixing that, the train step recompiles every few steps. Give the likely causes of both symptoms.
good_answer: Identical curves: the same PRNG key (or the same init key) is broadcast to every seed. Split a key into 32 and vmap over it (nnx.split_rngs or a stacked key array), and fold_in the step for per-step sampling keys.
Check: per-seed init params differ and per-seed samples differ at step 0.

Recompiles: something in the cache key changes. Common causes are shapes that vary with rollout length, a value passed through static_argnums or stored as a Python attribute on the NNX module (e.g. a LoRA scale or flag), a weak-type/dtype flip between a Python float and an array, or re-creating the jitted function or lambda each step.
Fix: pad to fixed length buckets, pass scale and hyperparameters as traced arrays, pass params as jit arguments (never closed over), and assert zero compiles after warmup with jax_log_compiles.
questions.verify: Show the toy-RL script's key handling and the zero-recompile assertion test. Claude asks you to read a jax_log_compiles line and name what changed.

questions.q: Your nightly re-run of weeks 1-2 gives SFT vs DPO paired differences of +2.1, +1.4 and -0.3 pass@1 points across 3 training seeds, and the two-level paired 95% CI is [0.1, 2.6]. The noise floor is 0.9 points. Is this a headline claim under the protocol, and what exactly do you write?
good_answer: The two-level bootstrap resamples seeds within each arm, then the shared item IDs, so the CI includes seed variance, not only item variance.
The mean gain of ~1.07 points is below 2 x noise floor = 1.8 points, and one seed has the opposite sign, so it fails two of the three criteria even though the CI excludes 0.
Report it as 'not established': show the per-seed differences, the CI and the noise-floor comparison, and do not call DPO better.
Do not use McNemar here: pass@1 estimated from many samples per item is not a single binary outcome per item. Use the paired bootstrap or Wilcoxon.

questions.q: Write the week-4 pre-registration note before the smoke run. Which fields must it contain under protocol 3.2.5 plus the RL-specific choices? Why must its commit predate the first run? Which choices made after seeing curves would invalidate a later headline?

questions.q: Compare loop (a), strictly on-policy, with loop (b), one-step async, where batch t+1 is sampled with the policy from step t-1 while batch t trains. What does (b) change in the importance ratio, clip fraction and KL estimates? What must you log, and why is (a) the sensible default on a single 4090?
good_answer: In (b), rollouts come from a behavior policy one update behind, so the ratio pi_theta/pi_behavior must use the log-probs the sampler saved at generation time, not values recomputed with current params. The ratio departs from 1, clipping becomes active, and the update is a truncated importance-weighted one
k1/k3 KL to the reference are estimated on samples from the behavior policy, not the current one, so they are slightly biased; the bias grows with staleness and LR
Log policy-version lag (staleness), clip fraction, ratio tails, and the sampler-trainer mismatch separately from the staleness effect

On one GPU in one process, sampling and training cannot run concurrently on the device, and holding the KV cache next to the optimizer state at the same time eats memory. So (b) mostly buys overlap with CPU verification. (a) keeps ratio = 1 (plain REINFORCE with a baseline) and removes a source of bias, which is why it is the default
