Donating the whole state, or keeping the KV cache alive into the train phase, so you hit deleted arrays or OOM at the week-5 config. Sizing the KV from the plan's Qwen2.5 numbers instead of Qwen3-1.7B's 8 KV heads makes this worse.

questions.q: Week 4 measured 75 s/step (sampling 45 s, reference 6 s, training 24 s). How many hours do the LR sweep (3 x 100 steps) and the main run (3 seeds x 300 steps) take on the 4090? Does that fit the week's nights, and what can go to a GPU burst under the budget rules?
good_answer: Sweep: 300 steps x 75 s = 6.25 h, one night.
Each 300-step seed takes 6.25 h, so 3 seeds take ~19 h, roughly 2 nights of 10 h. With the sweep and the mu=2 run that is ~4 nights of a 5-night week, with no slack for a rerun.

The extra seeds alone are a borderline case of the '>~2 nights' trigger. The main seed runs locally. The 2 extra seeds may burst only after the GPU dry run passed, sized from a step time measured on that GPU, and they are cut #2 if spend nears the cap.
Sampling is 60% of the step, so the highest-leverage optimization before buying cloud hours is the sampler (sub-batch size, early exit, buckets).
questions.verify: Compute it on paper, then compare it with the compute plan in your committed pre-registration note.

questions.q: Why do you pick the main-run LR from dev reward plus KL and entropy over ~100 steps rather than from test pass@1? And why is a good LoRA LR typically much higher than the full fine-tune LR for the same model?
good_answer: Selecting on test turns test into a dev set and biases the headline upward. Test stays untouched until the final eval.
100 steps on one seed is noisy, so the rule should prefer the highest LR whose KL and entropy stay healthy, not the single best reward point, and it is written down before you look at the curves.

With Adam, each LoRA parameter moves ~LR per step, but the induced change in W is the low-rank product scaled by alpha/r, starting from B=0. The effective weight change at a given LR is much smaller than in full FT.

Empirically (e.g. Thinking Machines' 'LoRA Without Regret'), the best LoRA LR is about 10x the full-FT LR and roughly rank-independent with alpha/r scaling. That sets the sweep range, but the sweep decides.
questions.verify: Explain it aloud. Claude probes with a sweep where the highest-reward LR also has KL rising fastest and asks what your rule picks.

questions.q: Two hours into the main run, mean completion length is pinned at 512 for nearly all samples and reward is near 0, though base pass@8 on dev was ~40%. What do you check first?
good_answer: Per-sequence EOS handling: Qwen3 chat turns end with <|im_end|> (id 151645), while <|endoftext|> is 151643. Checking only one id means sequences never stop. scripts/week0_jax_smoke.py passes both.
Chat template: enable_thinking=False must be applied, as in harness/prompts.py. Otherwise the model writes a long <think> block and hits the cap before the code.
Check the hit-max-tokens fraction and decode a few samples. The code extractor fails on truncated outputs, so the reward is 0.
Confirm that the done mask freezes finished sequences and that log-prob and loss masks stop at EOS (EOS included, pad excluded).
questions.verify: Explain it aloud, then show the sampler's EOS-id check and a decoded sample from the run JSONL.

questions.q: Reward has been flat for 100 steps and 85% of groups have zero variance. Using P(zero variance) = p^8 + (1-p)^8, what per-prompt pass rates does this suggest, and what is the pre-registered response?
good_answer: 85% zero variance means most prompts are near p=0 or p=1. For example, p=0.02 gives 0.98^8 = ~0.85.
This meets the early-kill condition (flat for 100 steps with >80% zero variance), so kill the run rather than wait.
Check which side it is: if nearly all-fail, the policy collapsed or extraction broke. If nearly all-pass, the training prompts are too easy.

Responses: filter prompts by measured pass rate, raise G, adjust temperature, or add a format-compatible tested set (e.g. APPS introductory, decontaminated). Any change of reward or data is a new pre-registered run.
questions.verify: Compute it on paper, then show the zero-variance fraction column in the run logs and the early-kill code path.

questions.q: The run logs mean |logp_sampler - logp_trainer| = 0.3 per token, against a week-3 baseline of ~1e-2. List the plausible causes in order of likelihood and the quick test for each.
good_answer: Temperature mismatch: the sampler returns log_softmax(logits/T) but the trainer uses T=1 (or the reverse). Test by recomputing trainer log-probs at the sampler's T on one batch.
Truncation: top-p or top-k left on for rollouts. RL must use top-p=1 and top-k off.
Wrong scale or adapter: the sampler used reference weights (LoRA scale 0) or a stale adapter. Check that the traced scale argument and the adapter arrays are the ones the trainer just updated.

Off-by-one alignment: the log-prob of token t taken from position t instead of t-1, or left-padding and position IDs that differ between KV-cache decode and the full forward. Test on one sequence by hand.
Each of these biases the ratio and the KL estimates, so fix it before trusting the clip fraction.
questions.verify: Explain it aloud, then rerun the week-3 sampler-vs-teacher-forced parity test on the RL config and show the number.

questions.q: Final held-out pass@1 (n=16 samples per test item): SFT 31.0, RL 34.2. Noise floor 1.3 points. Two-level paired 95% CI on the difference [1.1, 5.0]. Per-seed differences +3.5, +2.4, +3.7. Mean k3 KL stays under the bound. Does this meet the acceptance criteria, and what would make you downgrade it?
good_answer: The gain of 3.2 exceeds 2 x 1.3 = 2.6, the CI excludes 0, all 3 seed signs agree, and KL is bounded, so it meets acceptance.
All RL seeds start from the same merged SFT checkpoint, so the SFT arm has a single training seed and the bootstrap resamples RL seeds plus the shared items. Say so in the row.
Report the CI, per-seed differences, n, decoding config (T, top-p=1), sampler version, cost and the JSONL path in the results row.
Downgrade if the noise floor was measured with an older sampler, if test was used for any selection (LR or checkpoint), or if the gain disappears on MBPP+ or HumanEval+ (checked in week 6).
Per-item pass rates from 16 samples are not binary, so use the paired bootstrap, not McNemar.
questions.verify: Run the two-level bootstrap in harness/stats.py on the per-item JSONLs and show the CI and per-seed signs. Claude asks which line of the protocol each number satisfies.

questions.q: In the mu=2 run, predict the ratio and clip fraction on the first and second update of each batch, and what you expect to happen to KL and reward compared with mu=1.
good_answer: First update: pi_old equals the current policy (recomputed by the trainer), so rho = 1 and the clip fraction is 0 (or mismatch-level if pi_old comes from the sampler).
Second update: the policy has moved one step, so rho deviates from 1 and some tokens cross 1 +/- epsilon (e.g. 0.2). The clip fraction becomes nonzero and grows with LR.
Expect faster reward gains per sample and faster KL growth: each batch is reused, so sample efficiency rises, but so does the off-policy error.
If the clip fraction is large (above ~10-20%) or KL jumps, the LR is too high for mu=2. Compare at matched samples and at matched wall-clock.
questions.verify: Explain it aloud, then show the clip-fraction and KL curves from the mu=1 and mu=2 runs side by side.

questions.q: Qwen-family models are reported to gain on reasoning benchmarks under RLVR even with random or spurious rewards. Design the control that tells you your MBPP gain comes from the verifier reward and not from that effect.
good_answer: A random-reward arm: per-sample Bernoulli rewards independent of the completion, at the real arm's mean pass rate, with identical config, steps and seeds. It runs as exploratory in week 5 or as a pre-registered arm in week 6.

Mechanism to know: with rewards independent of samples, the expected advantage is zero, and the reported gains were traced to the clipping bias of PPO-style updates. So under mu=1 strictly on-policy (no active clipping) you should expect little effect, while mu=2 could show more.
A format-only reward arm (reward for a parseable ```python block) is the required week-6 control.

Decision rule written before launch: the real-reward gain over the random-reward arm must itself pass the protocol (2x noise floor, two-level CI excluding 0, sign agreement). Also check that the gain holds on the stricter MBPP+ tests.
questions.verify: Explain it aloud. Claude asks you to state the pre-registered decision rule and what you conclude if both arms gain equally.

questions.q: Your batch-mean k1 estimate goes negative and stays around -0.05 while k3 is about +0.02. Is this possible, and what would you check?
good_answer: Per-sample k1 = log(pi/pi_ref) can be negative, but its expectation under pi is KL(pi||pi_ref) >= 0. A persistently negative mean over 256 x ~300 tokens points to a bug.

Likely causes: the policy and reference swapped, or the tokens were sampled from a different distribution than the pi you evaluate (temperature or truncation mismatch), so the samples are not from pi.
k3 = r - 1 - log r is nonnegative per sample, so it can look healthy while k1 reveals the sampling mismatch.
Check: at step 0, with the fresh RL adapter's B = 0, pi equals pi_ref exactly and both k1 and k3 should be 0. Also confirm the reference is the merged-SFT base with scale 0.
questions.verify: Explain it aloud, then show the step-0 log line where k1 and k3 should be 0 and the reference-equals-SFT pytest.

Choosing the LR or checkpoint by looking at test, which invalidates the headline.

Calling a single-seed or sign-disagreeing result a headline instead of labeling it exploratory.

questions.q: Your week-0 dev run gives per-item pass rates p_i for Qwen3-1.7B (n=16 per item, mean pass@1 about 0.50). With group size G=8 and a binary reward, write the expected fraction of zero-variance groups, estimate it from the data, and say why it is far above p^8+(1-p)^8 at p=0.5.
good_answer: P(zero variance | item i) = p_i^8 + (1-p_i)^8; the expected fraction is its average over the items drawn into batches.

At p=0.5 it is 2/256 = 0.008, but on dev about 30% of items are never solved and about 33% always solved in 16 samples, so the item average is about 0.70 (Jensen: the function is convex, and the rates are bimodal).
Plugging in p_hat^8 is biased upward. The unbiased per-item estimate is [C(c,8) + C(16-c,8)] / C(16,8), the same combinatorics as unbiased pass@k.

Zero-variance groups get zero advantage and no gradient but still cost rollout tokens, so at base only ~30% of the 32 prompts per step (~9-10) carry signal. Re-measure after SFT, since the training policy is SFT, not base.
Partial credit (fraction of the 3 MBPP asserts passed) makes all-equal groups rarer. That is one way it could help that has nothing to do with shaping, and the note should separate the two.

questions.q: Derive the per-token gradient weight that standard GRPO gives a token in response o_i, given the 1/|o_i| length normalization and A_i = (r_i - mean)/std. What length drift does it cause on wrong answers, and what does Dr. GRPO change to remove it?
good_answer: The GRPO loss averages over tokens within each sequence and then over the G sequences, so each token of o_i gets weight A_i / (G |o_i|) times its ratio or log-prob gradient.

For a wrong answer (A_i < 0), a longer response spreads the penalty over more tokens, so each token is pushed down less. Long wrong answers are under-penalized and failure lengths can grow. For correct answers, shorter responses get a larger per-token push.
Dr. GRPO replaces 1/|o_i| with a constant (sum over all tokens divided by a fixed L_max or token budget) and uses A_i = r_i - mean, with no division by std.

Dropping std matters because binary-reward std is sqrt(p(1-p)). At 1 correct out of 8, the correct sample's advantage is 0.875/0.331 = 2.65 instead of 0.875, so near-all-fail and near-all-pass groups get upweighted (a question-difficulty bias). Zero-variance groups must give A=0 and no NaN in both variants.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then point Claude to the lines in your GRPO loss where each normalization happens and show the pytest with hand-computed values on 2 groups x 3 samples for both variants.

questions.q: Why does this experiment need a format-only control arm, and what does the error breakdown in your week-0 dev results say about how big a gain format and interface fixes alone could give?

In the week-0 dev run, 530 of 3200 samples were 'error' (17%). Only 6 were SyntaxError. About 174 were NameError (often the wrong function name, e.g. list_tuple vs list_to_tuple) and 230 TypeError (many with the wrong number of arguments), so interface fixes alone could lift pass@1 by several points.
Qwen-family models have shown gains under spurious or random rewards, so RL here can elicit behavior the model already has. The control measures how much of the sparse-arm gain is elicitation.

If train looks like dev (about 63% of items always or never solved by base), only about 100 items give non-zero-variance groups, and the share shifts as the policy learns. Measure it on train after SFT, not on dev.

At this many epochs, training reward measures memorization as much as learning. Only held-out MBPP test, MBPP+ and HumanEval+ can support the claim, so held-out pass@1 every N steps is the curve to watch.

A Wilcoxon signed-rank test on seed-averaged per-item rates is a cross-check.

The claim needs all three: gain > 2x the noise floor (SD of the metric across 3 sampling seeds on one checkpoint, re-measured after the week-3 sampler change), two-level CI excluding 0, and the same sign on every training seed.
There are well over 5 comparisons this week (arms vs SFT, vs control, vs each other, x MBPP/MBPP+/HumanEval+), so apply Holm to the pre-registered set and label the rest exploratory.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then point Claude to the two-level resampling function you added to harness/stats.py in week 3 and run it on two checkpoints' per-item JSONLs.

questions.q: Your best arm beats base on pass@1 on the 200-item subset, but the base pass@k curve crosses above it at k=16-32. What does that support, and what limits the claim at k=32 with n=64?
good_answer: The crossover matches Yue et al. 2025: RLVR concentrates probability on solutions the base already finds, which raises pass@1 but can shrink coverage, so the base solves more items given enough samples.

Unbiased pass@k = 1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k), averaged over items. At n=64, k=32 any item with c >= ~5 is near 1 and an item with c=1 contributes exactly 0.5, so the curve is set by a small set of hard items with few successes. The item-level CI is wide and the comparison has little power.
The claim needs bootstrap CIs at every k, resampling items and the 3 best-arm seeds. Overlapping bands at k=32 mean no crossover claim. k=64 needs n=128.

All models must use the same decoding config (T, top-p/top-k). The week-0 baselines used top_p=0.8, top_k=20, which may differ from the training sampler, so re-run base under the week-6 config and state it in the row.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show Claude the pass@k plot and the code computing the estimator per item and its bootstrap bands.

questions.q: On the first H100 run, the first ~10 steps are 5x slower than steady state, even though the persistent compilation cache was populated on the 4090 with the same JAX version. Why, and what do you change in launch.sh?
good_answer: The cache key includes the HLO, compile options, backend/platform version and device kind, so sm_89 (4090) entries never hit on sm_90 (H100). Each shape bucket compiles again the first time it is used, and buckets appear lazily over the first steps.

One compile per bucket is expected. More than that means a dynamic shape or a Python-attribute flag is retracing, so check with jax_log_compiles. Also note that only compiles longer than jax_persistent_cache_min_compile_time_secs are cached.

Point the cache at storage that survives the instance (a bucket or persistent disk, one directory per hardware type), so the 3 parallel H100 runs and any resumed runs reuse it. Warm every bucket with a dummy step before the timed loop, and exclude warmup from tokens/s.

The kernels differ too: XLA autotuning picks different GEMM and attention implementations on H100, so numerics shift slightly. Compare the sampler-trainer log-prob mismatch on H100 with the 4090 value before trusting the curves.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show Claude the jax_log_compiles output from the first minutes of the burst log and the cache-dir setting in launch.sh.

questions.q: Size and price the training burst: 9 runs on 3x H100 SXM at ~$2.5/h, starting from your measured week-5 step time. Then say what you cut first if the running total nears the $400 planned bound.
good_answer: Scale the measured 4090 step time. Decode is bandwidth-bound (~3.35 TB/s vs ~1 TB/s), so rollouts may run up to ~3x faster, less for prefill, training and CPU verification. At ~2-3 h per run: 3 rounds of 3 parallel runs is about 6-9 h wall clock and 18-27 GPU-h, roughly $45-70, inside the plan's $40-80 and the $150 per-burst cap.
Add setup, compile warmup, idle and eval-upload time, and log real accelerator_hours and cost_usd.
Use spot only if kill-and-resume has been tested. With checkpoints every 20 min, a preemption costs at most ~20 min per run. Auto-shutdown and a billing alert are mandatory.
Cut order from section 3.4: week-8 burst seeds first, then week-5 extra seeds, then the week-6 n=128 high-k eval, then the 12B teacher (already off). Never touch the week-13 reservation.
questions.verify: Write the compute plan in the pre-registration note and have Claude check the arithmetic against your week-5 step time and the cost_usd rows.

weeks.exit_check: You are done with this week when the RLVR note draft states whether the alternative reward beats both sparse and the format-only control on MBPP test and HumanEval+ (two-level paired CIs, noise floor, sign agreement over 3 seeds), quantifies the MBPP+ and hidden-test hacking gaps, and every number traces to a logged result row with cost filled in.
pitfalls: Reporting arm-vs-SFT gains without the format-only control, so fixing function names, signatures and format on Qwen3 is mistaken for learning correctness.
Leaking MBPP+ or the hidden-test subset into the reward or into checkpoint selection, which destroys the held-out hacking measurement.
Reading rising training reward on a 274-item pool reused ~35 times as progress, when held-out pass@1 is flat.
Launching the burst before the pre-registration commit or without a tested kill-and-resume, or comparing models at different decoding configs (T, top-p/top-k), or pass@k near k=n/2 without CIs.

weeks.title: Agents + agent eval
weeks.theme: Before training a multi-turn agent with RL in week 8, you need a task set, a sandboxed tool environment, a token-exact multi-turn rollout and an eval that can tell whether tools actually help Qwen3-1.7B.
goals: 50-100 frozen spine tasks built from MBPP (Mon, before any agent code): eval tasks from dev/test only, preferring test items with MBPP+ tests so the hidden checker is stricter than anything the tool runs, and warm-start/week-8 training tasks from train only. Each task has a checker that passes the reference solution and fails a known-wrong one.

Tools implemented as a sandboxed run-code/run-visible-tests tool in a spawn-based subprocess pool (workers never import jax) with resource limits and timeouts, returning strings truncated to a fixed token budget. BM25 only if the tasks need it.

Multi-turn v1 working by Tue: each turn re-prefills the full concatenated token-ID context through the tested prefill path. The chat template is applied at the token level, each turn has a token cap, sequences stop on the tool-call stop IDs, and the token-ID span of every inserted tool output is logged.

Eval of LLM-only vs LLM+tools vs a matched-budget control on the same task IDs, 3 trials per task, paired CIs over tasks, and a ~10-category failure taxonomy hand-coded on 50 failures. Optionally an API model as a stronger subject, and an LLM judge only for one dimension that needs it, validated against 30-50 hand labels.
Overnight warm-start generation on train tasks only, keeping ~200 successful trajectories for week 8, with counts per task and per turn count recorded.
Stretch: in-cache continuation that matches a full prefill of the same token IDs.
deliverables: Task file with frozen task IDs, prompts, visible test, hidden checker and split provenance, plus pytests that each checker passes the reference and fails a known-wrong solution.

Agent env module: tool sandbox, truncation, token-level template, stop IDs, span logging, per-turn caps. Pytests check that the multi-turn context equals the concatenation of sampled IDs and inserted tool IDs, that token-level template construction matches the tokenizer's template for a single-turn prompt, and that the sampler records zero recompiles after warmup.
Agent eval table: success rate per arm with bootstrap CIs over tasks, paired differences, turns used, tool-error rate, tokens per task, decoding config and cost.
Failure taxonomy with category definitions, counts per arm and example trajectory IDs.
Saved trajectories (JSONL of token IDs, spans, tool outputs, outcomes, task IDs) for the eval runs and the warm-start pool.
Stretch: in-cache continuation with a parity test on a ragged batch.
learned: You can explain why multi-turn RL data must stay as token IDs end to end, and show concrete cases where re-tokenizing or re-templating text gives different IDs.
You can compute the FLOP and memory cost of re-prefilling 2-3 turns and decide when in-cache continuation is worth building.
You can keep a multi-turn JAX rollout free of recompiles by truncating tool outputs to a fixed budget and padding whole contexts to a few length buckets.
You can build a code-execution sandbox that is bounded, does not leak or expose the hidden checker, and is safe to run from a JAX process.
You can design an agent eval with a control that separates execution feedback from extra attempts and tokens, and analyze it with paired statistics over tasks.
You can build a failure taxonomy specific enough to suggest week-8 reward or environment changes.
You can validate an LLM judge against hand labels on one dimension and report its agreement.

questions.q: Why must the multi-turn rollout never decode to text, append the tool output, and re-tokenize or re-apply the chat template? Give two concrete ways it breaks with Qwen3 and say what goes wrong in week-8 training if you do it.
good_answer: BPE is not concatenation-invariant: encode(a + b) can differ from encode(a) + encode(b) at the boundary (whitespace or newline runs after a closing code fence merge into different tokens), and decode then encode of sampled IDs does not always round-trip.

Re-applying Qwen3's chat template to the text history can rewrite earlier assistant turns. The template handles <think> blocks in past assistant messages differently from the generation prompt (with enable_thinking=False it inserts an empty think block), so the context no longer equals what was sampled.

The trainer then computes log-probs for IDs the sampler never produced, so importance ratios and KL are computed on the wrong sequence, and the logged tool-output spans no longer line up with the week-8 mask.
Fix: build the template at the token level (<|im_start|>, <|im_end|> and role headers as IDs), encode each tool output once on its own, append IDs, and log each span.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show Claude a pytest that finds a boundary case where re-tokenization differs, and the pytest that the env's context equals the logged concatenation of IDs.

questions.q: Estimate the cost of re-prefilling the full context each turn for a 3-turn trajectory whose contexts are ~600, ~1200 and ~1800 tokens on Qwen3-1.7B, for 75 tasks x 3 trials. Is in-cache continuation worth building this week?
good_answer: Prefill FLOPs are about 2 x N x T: 2 x 1.72e9 x (600+1200+1800) is about 12.4 TFLOP per trajectory, versus ~6.2 TFLOP if each token were prefilled once. Attention adds roughly 4 x L x T^2 x d per prefill, small at T <= 2k.
At an effective ~65 TFLOP/s on the 4090 (~40% of ~165 TFLOP/s dense bf16) that is ~0.19 s per trajectory, ~40 s for all 225.

Decode is bandwidth-bound: each decode step re-reads ~3.4 GB of weights (shared across the batch) plus every sequence's KV cache, so generating a few hundred tokens per turn costs far more wall time than the re-prefill.
Conclusion: at 2-3 turns and <= 2k tokens, re-prefill is cheap and in-cache continuation is a stretch. It pays off only with many turns or long contexts.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then time a 3-turn rollout with Claude and read the prefill share from a jax.profiler trace.

questions.q: Your first multi-turn eval logs dozens of 'Compiling ...' lines per task. What causes it, and how do you design the shapes so the whole eval compiles a small, fixed number of programs?
good_answer: Each turn's context has a different length, so passing it unpadded to the jitted prefill or sampler creates a new shape, and a new trace, for every distinct length (and for every distinct batch size at the tail of the task list).

Truncate tool outputs to a fixed token budget so lengths are bounded. Pad the whole concatenated context to a few buckets (e.g. 512/1024/2048) with an attention mask and per-sequence positions, and fix the batch size by padding the last batch.
Expected compiles: one prefill per bucket and one decode loop per (batch, max_len), all paid during warmup.
Assert zero recompiles after warmup with jax_log_compiles or a compile counter, and make sure the turn index, LoRA scale or stop IDs are traced arrays, not Python values baked into the trace.
questions.verify: Show Claude the zero-recompile assertion passing over a full eval pass, plus the list of compiled bucket shapes.

questions.q: Design the sandbox for the run-code/run-tests tool. What limits do you set, how is the pool created, and how do you make sure the agent cannot see or tamper with the checker that decides success?
good_answer: Each execution runs in its own subprocess with resource limits (RLIMIT_AS, RLIMIT_CPU, RLIMIT_FSIZE, RLIMIT_NPROC), a wall-clock timeout that kills the process group, and a fresh temp dir. Blocking network needs a namespace or container (e.g. unshare -n or bwrap), since rlimits cannot do it.
The pool uses multiprocessing spawn or forkserver (or starts before importing jax), and workers never import jax, because forking a process that has initialized CUDA is unsafe.

The tool runs only the visible example test or the agent's own tests. The success checker runs the hidden asserts and MBPP+ tests in a separate process after the episode, from files never placed in the agent's working dir, so the agent cannot read, edit or monkeypatch them.
Tool output is a string truncated to a fixed token budget (e.g. head plus the last N tokens of a traceback), so shapes stay bounded and huge outputs cannot blow up the context.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show Claude a pytest where a submitted program tries to read the checker file, loop forever, fork-bomb and allocate 10 GB, and all four are contained.

questions.q: Your tool runs the visible example test. Your first checker draft used the same three MBPP asserts the training verifier uses, two of them hidden. Why is a checker that equals what the tool can run a bad agent eval, and how should tool tests and checker tests relate?
good_answer: If the tool can run exactly the checker, the agent can iterate until it passes, so success measures retry-with-oracle, and hardcoding the tested cases is rewarded. The tools arm wins for a reason that does not transfer.
The tool should expose a strict subset (the shown assert, or only tests the agent writes), and the checker should use held-out tests: the other MBPP asserts plus MBPP+ extended tests where available.
Report how often the final code passes the visible test but fails the checker, per arm. That gap is the agent-level hacking signal week 8 will track.
Freeze this split per task in the task file, and test that no hidden test string appears in the prompt or in any tool output.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show Claude the task-file schema and the leakage pytest that greps prompts and tool outputs for hidden test strings.

questions.q: You find LLM+tools beats LLM-only by 15 points. Why is this comparison confounded, and what control arm do you add so the claim is about execution feedback?
good_answer: The tools arm gets up to 3 turns, so it has more attempts and more generated tokens. Part of the gain could come from extra samples or self-revision, not from what the test output says.

Control: matched-budget LLM-only, either best-of-3 from independent samples judged only by the visible test (the same information the tool gives), or self-revision for the same number of turns with no execution output inserted.
Optional second control: the tools arm with tool output replaced by an uninformative string of the same token length, which keeps turns and shapes fixed.
Report all arms on the same task IDs with paired CIs and tokens per task, so the claim is gain at a matched budget.
questions.verify: Explain aloud while Claude probes which arm should win under each hypothesis, then check that the eval table contains the control arm.

questions.q: With 75 tasks and 3 trials each, how do you compute the CI on the LLM vs LLM+tools difference, why not McNemar, and roughly how wide would an unpaired CI be at a 50% success rate?
good_answer: For each task, compute a success rate from the 3 trials in each arm, take paired per-task differences, and bootstrap over task IDs (95% CI), or use Wilcoxon signed-rank on the per-task differences.
McNemar needs one binary outcome per item per arm. Three trials give rates, so McNemar only applies if you use trial 1 alone.
A single proportion at n=75, p=0.5 has a CI of about 1.96 x sqrt(0.25/75), roughly +/-11 pts. An unpaired difference is about +/-16 pts, which is why pairing is needed.

There is no training seed here, so a one-level paired bootstrap over tasks (optionally resampling trials within each task) is the protocol. With more than ~5 comparisons, use Holm or label them exploratory.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then run the paired bootstrap from harness/stats.py on the eval JSONL with Claude.

questions.q: Agent trajectories never stop after a tool call: the model keeps generating past the call, invents a fake tool result, and answers. What is wrong in the rollout, and what test catches it?
good_answer: The stop condition only checks EOS (<|im_end|>), so the sampler does not stop at the end of the tool call (e.g. Qwen3's </tool_call> token, or whatever delimiter your protocol uses) and the model hallucinates the response.

Add the tool-call end ID(s) as per-sequence stop IDs in the sampler, stop that sequence, run the tool, and insert the real output as token IDs where the template puts tool responses (for Qwen3, a <tool_response> block inside a user turn; check the tokenizer's template).
Check that your token-level template matches Qwen3's template for tool turns and the logged enable_thinking setting. A mismatch moves the model off its trained format.
Test: on a scripted trajectory, assert the sampled span ends exactly at the stop ID and the next span is the logged tool-output span.
questions.verify: Show Claude the pytest on a scripted trajectory, plus one saved trajectory from before and one from after the fix.

questions.q: Implement the in-cache continuation stretch: what state must be per-sequence, how do you write appended chunks into the cache under jit, and what exactly must the parity test compare?
good_answer: Per-sequence write positions as an int array [B] and per-sequence RoPE positions that count only real tokens. A scalar position breaks as soon as sequences in a batch have different lengths.

Write each appended chunk, padded to a fixed bucket with a mask, using a vmapped lax.dynamic_update_slice (or a scatter) into the [B, T_max, KV_heads, head_dim] cache, so shapes stay static and max_len covers all turns.
The attention mask has to exclude padded slots inside the cache, not just at the end, because padded chunks leave holes.

Parity: logits and log-probs after continuation must equal a full prefill of the same token IDs (at highest matmul precision, within tolerance) for every sequence in a ragged batch, not just sequence 0.
questions.verify: Show Claude the parity pytest on a ragged batch with 3 turns, and the zero-recompile check across turns.

questions.q: You want an LLM judge to score one dimension (for example 'does the agent use test output to fix its code'). How do you validate it before using its scores in the eval table?
good_answer: Hand-label 30-50 trajectories on that dimension first, blind to arm, using a written rubric. Tune the judge prompt on a few of them and measure agreement on the rest.
For pairwise judgments, run both orderings and average them to remove position bias.
Report agreement (and Cohen's kappa) against the hand labels, broken down per arm. If agreement is low, drop the judge and use hand labels or drop the dimension.
Keep the judge on that one dimension. Success is always decided by the code checker, never by the judge.
questions.verify: Explain aloud; Claude asks for the agreement table and probes the disagreements on 3 examples.

questions.q: Overnight you collect warm-start trajectories by sampling many attempts per train task and keeping the successes. What biases does this pool carry into week-8 SFT, and how do you limit them?
good_answer: Success filtering over-represents easy tasks and short, one-turn trajectories. Tasks the base already solves dominate, so the warm start teaches little about using tool feedback.
Cap successes per task, record counts per task and per number of turns, and prefer trajectories that used a tool output before succeeding.
Use only train-split tasks and check that no eval task ID or hidden test appears in the pool.

If an API or teacher model writes trajectories, check its terms and tokenize each segment once into the Qwen3 token-level template with logged spans. Label them off-policy (fine for SFT, but there are no sampler log-probs for RL) and report the source mix.
questions.verify: Show Claude the per-task and per-turn count histograms and the split-provenance check on the warm-start JSONL.

weeks.exit_check: You are done with this week when the agent eval table compares LLM-only, LLM+tools and a matched-budget control on the same frozen tasks with paired CIs over tasks and a hidden checker the tool cannot run, a hand-coded failure taxonomy explains the main failure modes, and the saved token-ID trajectories pass the span and context-concatenation tests week-8 masking depends on.
pitfalls: Re-tokenizing concatenated text or re-applying the chat template between turns, which silently corrupts log-probs and mask spans for week 8.
Letting the tool run the same tests as the checker, or letting the agent see or modify hidden tests, or using dev/test tasks for warm-start data.
Per-turn context lengths with no buckets, so the sampler recompiles for every task.
Crediting tools for a gain that comes from extra turns and tokens, because no matched-budget control was run.

weeks.title: Agent RL (2-3 turns)
weeks.theme: Week 8 trains the week-7 agent with the week 4-6 GRPO code, so you learn what changes when rollouts contain tokens the policy did not generate.
goals: Multi-turn GRPO (or the RLOO variant chosen in week 5) runs end to end on Qwen3-1.7B with 2-3 turns and a per-turn token cap. Token IDs are kept end to end: the chat template is applied at the token level and concatenated text is never re-tokenized.

The three tool-token mask tests pass. (a) The per-token loss and advantage at tool positions are exactly 0. (b) With input tokens fixed, changing the target labels or advantages at tool positions leaves loss and gradient bit-identical. (c) The mask covers exactly the token-ID spans the env logged when it inserted the tool output.

SFT warm start on the successful trajectories collected in week 7 (target ~200; report the actual count), with the same model-token mask on the SFT loss. Then merge the adapter and add a fresh RL adapter, as in section 3.1.

Outcome-only vs outcome + valid-call bonus at matched steps with 3 seeds per arm (2 local + 1 in a GPU burst). Under cut #1 this drops to 2 local seeds, labeled exploratory. A pre-registration note is committed before launch.

Step time is measured on the multi-turn config before runs are sized. Turns per episode, tool-error rate, zero-variance group fraction, model-token length and sampler-trainer log-prob mismatch are logged every step.
Fri PM is kept as a buffer. Scorecard row 3 is filled with linked evidence, and cost_usd is updated in the README.
deliverables: Pre-registration note committed before launch: hypothesis, arms, headline metric (held-out outcome pass@1), n, decision rule, KL placement, on-policy/async choice, and a compute plan (runs × measured hours, accelerator, cost).
tests/ covering mask properties (a), (b) and (c), plus a token-ID round-trip test across turn boundaries (trainer input IDs == sampled IDs + env-inserted IDs).
Per-seed learning curves plus the mean for both arms. Held-out outcome pass@1 with a 95% CI, the two-level paired bootstrap, per-seed paired differences and the sign check.
Failure analysis of trajectories, or the fallback: a verified pipeline plus a written 'why no learning' diagnosis.
Results rows with git SHA, config hash, decoding config, seeds, accelerator, accelerator_hours, cost_usd and per-item JSONL paths. Scorecard row 3.
Optional: a test-tampering probe in which the agent can write to the test file, with the tampering rate logged against a pristine hidden copy of the tests.
learned: You can explain why tool-output tokens get no loss but still shape gradients through attention, and you can write a test that checks the mask without being fooled by that effect.
You can size a multi-turn rollout batch from KV-cache arithmetic for Qwen3-1.7B on a 24 GB card, including JAX's default preallocation fraction.
You can predict the fraction of zero-variance GRPO groups from per-prompt pass rates, and use it to judge whether a warm start is too strong.
You can compute group advantages and a KL penalty on model tokens only, and explain how loss normalization creates a length bias when episodes span several turns.
You can design a shaped-reward comparison whose headline is the unshaped outcome, so a hacked bonus cannot pass for progress.
You can trace sampler-trainer mismatch at turn boundaries to tokenization, position-ID or template bugs.
You can keep a variable-length multi-turn loop at a fixed, predicted number of compiled programs.
You can spread seeds across local and burst hardware so the arm comparison stays paired and is not confounded with hardware.

questions.q: Tool output tokens get loss weight 0, yet changing their input IDs changes the gradient on later model tokens. Why is that correct, and what exact test proves your mask is right without being fooled by this effect?
good_answer: Tool tokens are context. Later model tokens attend to them, so their input IDs legitimately change the activations and gradients of the tokens that do carry loss.
The mask zeroes only the per-token loss term and advantage at tool positions. It does not detach the inputs, and it should not.

Property (b): keep input_ids fixed, change only the target labels and the advantage values at tool positions, and assert that loss and every gradient leaf are bit-identical (jnp.array_equal, not allclose).
Apply the mask with jnp.where rather than multiplying by 0. If a masked position produces inf or NaN (for example a pad label), 0 * NaN is NaN, while where() keeps the result exactly 0.
Also assert that the per-token loss vector is exactly 0 at tool positions (a), and that the mask's True spans equal the env-logged spans (c).
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show and run the pytest for property (b). Claude asks what would go wrong if the test changed input_ids instead, and what happens with mask multiplication when the label is out of range.

questions.q: Write the pytest for mask property (c): the loss mask covers exactly the token spans the env logged when it inserted tool outputs. What inputs make it a real test rather than a tautology?
good_answer: The env records (start, end) token indices for each inserted span (tool output plus the template tokens it adds) at insertion time, in code that is independent of the trainer's mask builder.

Build the mask with the trainer's own function. Assert that every env-inserted span and all prompt/system tokens are False. Assert that every sampled token is True, including the sampled end-of-turn/EOS token.
Assert that sum(mask) equals the number of tokens the sampler reported generating for that sequence.
The fixture should cover at least 2 turns, a tool output cut at the truncation budget, left padding, and an episode that finishes early (done mask), because those are where off-by-one errors live.
questions.verify: Show the pytest and run it. Claude asks which fixture case catches an off-by-one at the end of a truncated tool output, then breaks the mask builder by one token to see if the test fails.

questions.q: For one task, G=4 episodes get outcome rewards [1, 0, 0, 1]. Compute the GRPO advantages (mean/std normalized) and the RLOO advantages. Which tokens do they apply to, and where does the KL term go if you use the k3 estimator?
good_answer: GRPO: mean 0.5 and std 0.5 (population std), so the advantages are [+1, −1, −1, +1]. If the code uses the sample std (≈0.577), they are ±0.866. Know which one your code uses.
RLOO: A_i = r_i − mean of the other G−1 rewards. That gives 1 − 1/3 = 2/3 for the successes and 0 − 2/3 = −2/3 for the failures. In general A_i = G/(G−1)·(r_i − r̄).
Each episode's scalar advantage is broadcast to every model-generated token in all of its turns. Tool and template tokens get 0 through the mask.

k3 per token: with ρ = π_ref/π_θ evaluated at the sampled token, k3 = ρ − log ρ − 1 ≥ 0. Its expectation under samples from π_θ is KL(π_θ‖π_ref). It is computed and averaged only over model tokens, and it goes in the loss or the reward according to the pre-registered placement.
The reference here is the merged-SFT base with the RL adapter at scale 0, passed as a traced argument.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then run the advantage function from week 4 on this group in a pytest and compare. Claude probes what changes when the bonus makes rewards non-binary.

questions.q: With group size G=8, predict the fraction of zero-variance groups for prompts whose true pass rate is 0.5, 0.8 and 0.9. What does this imply if the SFT warm start lifts most training prompts to ~0.9?
good_answer: P(zero variance) = p^G + (1−p)^G.

A zero-variance group has advantage 0 for every member under both GRPO and RLOO, so ~43% of the batch adds no policy gradient at p=0.9. With std normalization, the numerator is 0, so eps in the denominator does not rescue it.

Implications: filter or reweight prompts toward intermediate pass rates, use a weaker or shorter warm start, or grow G. Log the fraction every step. The batch-level fraction is the mean of this formula over the prompts' own pass rates.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the zero-variance fraction logged over the first 20 steps and with per-prompt pass rates from the warm-started checkpoint.

questions.q: Compute the bf16 KV-cache bytes per token for Qwen3-1.7B (look up layers, KV heads and head_dim in its config.json) and the largest number of 2048-token episodes you can hold at once on the 4090. Can you sample 256 rollouts at 2k context in one call?
good_answer: The config gives 28 layers, 8 KV heads and head_dim 128. Per token: 28 × 8 × 128 × 2 (K and V) × 2 bytes = 114,688 B ≈ 112 KiB.

Weights are ≈1.72B params (tied embeddings) ≈ 3.4 GB in bf16. By default JAX preallocates 75% of the 24 GB (~18 GB) unless XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION is changed. After LoRA/Adam state, logits and decode workspace, that leaves roughly 12-16 GB for KV.
A fixed-max_len cache reserves the full 2048 slots per episode whatever its actual length. 14 GB / (2048 × 114,688 B) ≈ 60 episodes, so about 55-68 depending on the headroom.
256 × 2048 × 114,688 B ≈ 60 GB, so no. Sample in waves of ~32-64 (or shorten the context) and free the cache before the training step.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the measured peak from a sampler run (device memory_stats or the week-3 memory test) at that wave size.

questions.q: Sampler-trainer log-prob mismatch is ~1e-2 on turn-1 tokens but jumps above 1 nat on the first few tokens of turns 2 and 3. List the likely causes in order and the test that isolates each.
good_answer: Re-tokenizing concatenated text: boundary tokens merge or split differently, so the trainer scores tokens that were never sampled. Test: assert that the trainer input IDs exactly equal the concatenation of sampled IDs and env-inserted IDs.

Position IDs or attention mask wrong after concatenation with left padding (positions restart, or pad tokens are counted). Test: compare the teacher-forced log-probs of one unpadded sequence with the same sequence inside a padded batch.
The new turn's chat-template tokens are inserted differently in the sampler and trainer paths. Test: log and diff the token IDs around every boundary.

With in-cache continuation, a stale or mis-offset KV write position. Test: continuation vs a full prefill of the same IDs. Truncated or temperature-mismatched sampler log-probs would show up on turn 1 too, so they rank lower here.
questions.verify: Explain aloud. Claude gives a mismatch trace per position and asks which test you run first and why.

questions.q: An episode's outcome advantage is broadcast to all of its model tokens across turns. Compare normalizing the loss by each episode's own model-token count vs by a constant (Dr. GRPO style). Which one biases toward shorter correct and longer wrong episodes, and which length must you count in multi-turn?
good_answer: Per-episode mean: every episode gets the same total weight, so each token in an episode of length L gets A/L. With L=100 vs 400, a short correct episode gets 4× the per-token push.
For negative A, long episodes are penalized less per token, so being wrong at length is cheap. That is the bias: short when right, long when wrong.
Dividing by a constant (a fixed token budget) gives every token the same weight A/C and removes the bias. Token-level normalization over the batch (DAPO style) mostly does too.
L must be the number of masked model tokens, not the sequence length with tool and template tokens. Otherwise episodes with long tool outputs get diluted gradients.
Multi-turn makes the bias sharper because lengths vary with turn count, so log model-token length per arm.
questions.verify: Derive on paper with two toy episodes of length 100 and 400, then point to the normalization line in your loss code and the pytest that checks it.

questions.q: Design the outcome-only vs outcome + valid-call bonus comparison so that a model that learns to spam harmless valid calls cannot look like a win.
good_answer: The pre-registered headline metric is held-out outcome pass@1 (tests pass), never the training reward, which includes the bonus. Both arms are compared at matched steps.
Cap the bonus per episode and keep it well below the outcome reward (e.g. ≤0.1 vs 1).
Shaping that is not potential-based (F = γΦ(s′) − Φ(s), Ng et al. 1999) can change the optimal policy. A per-call bonus is not potential-based, so expect distortion and measure for it.
Log calls per episode, turns per episode, tool-error rate and the reward split into outcome and bonus per arm. Inspect ~30 bonus-arm trajectories for degenerate calls.
Decide using the two-level paired bootstrap over seeds and items, the 2× noise-floor rule and per-seed sign agreement.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the pre-registration note. Claude plays a reviewer who claims the bonus arm wins on reward.

questions.q: You run 2 seeds per arm on the 4090 and 1 per arm on a rented H100. How do you assign seeds and analyze them so hardware does not confound the arm comparison?
good_answer: Pair by seed index: seed k of both arms runs on the same hardware with the same data order and PRNG key, so the within-pair difference cancels hardware numerics. Seeds 1-2 of both arms run locally and seed 3 of both arms runs on the burst.
Never put all of one arm on the burst and all of the other locally.

Analyze with the two-level paired bootstrap (resample seeds within each arm, then resample shared item IDs). Report the per-seed paired differences and the sign check, and evaluate every checkpoint with the same local eval harness.
Record the accelerator in every results row. If cut #1 is taken, there are 2 seeds, the result is labeled exploratory, and no headline claim is made.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the two-level bootstrap function you added to harness/stats.py in week 3 (today the file only has the single-level paired_bootstrap). Claude asks what it resamples first.

questions.q: Bonus arm: training reward rises steadily, tool-error rate drops to 0, turns per episode sits at the maximum, and held-out outcome pass@1 is flat. Diagnose it and say what you would show in the write-up.

questions.q: Why must XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=8 be set before import jax, and what happens to your sharding test if it is set too late?
good_answer: XLA reads the flag when the CPU backend initializes, at the first backend use after import. After that the device count is fixed for the process.
Set too late, jax.devices() returns 1 CPU device, every NamedSharding is trivially replicated, and sharded == unsharded passes for the wrong reason.
So assert len(jax.devices()) == 8 at the start of the test.

Set it in the shell or at the top of conftest.py before any jax import, or set jax.config.update('jax_num_cpu_devices', 8) before backend init on newer JAX (verify). Run the sharding tests in their own process so another test file can't initialize JAX first.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show conftest.py and the assertion line, and run the test once with the flag removed to see it fail.

questions.q: For a 300M-parameter decoder trained with Adam in mixed precision (fp32 master weights, fp32 grads, fp32 m and v), compute per-chip memory for parameters, grads and optimizer state under pure DP and under FSDP on 8 chips. Compare with v5e's 16 GB HBM per chip, and redo it for 1.7B.
good_answer: Bytes per param: 4 (master) + 4 (grad) + 4 (m) + 4 (v) = 16, plus 2 if a bf16 compute copy is kept.
DP: 300M × 16 B ≈ 4.8 GB on every chip, plus activations.
FSDP over 8: ≈0.6 GB per chip of sharded state, plus the all-gathered bf16 weights of the layer(s) in flight.
At 300M both fit in 16 GB, and activations (batch × seq × d × layers, cut by remat) usually dominate. At 1.7B, DP state is ~27 GB and does not fit, while FSDP-8 is ~3.4 GB per chip.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with compile().memory_analysis() (verify the API) for the train step on the fake 8-device mesh.

questions.q: Per step, how many bytes does each device send for gradient sync under DP with ring all-reduce, and under FSDP (all-gather in forward, all-gather again in backward, reduce-scatter of grads)? Express it with P = bytes of parameters (or gradients) and n devices.
good_answer: Ring all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather, each (n−1)/n · P, so ≈2(n−1)/n · P per device.

FSDP: all-gather params in forward, (n−1)/n · P; again in backward unless they are kept, (n−1)/n · P; reduce-scatter grads, (n−1)/n · P. Total ≈3(n−1)/n · P, about 1.5× DP, in exchange for ~n× less state memory.
Use the dtype each collective actually moves: bf16 params are all-gathered, while grads may be reduced in fp32 or bf16. This changes P.
Expect all-reduce in the DP HLO and all-gather plus reduce-scatter in the FSDP HLO.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then dump the compiled HLO for each spec on the fake mesh and find the collectives by name. Claude asks you to predict them first.

questions.q: Your sharded loss matches unsharded to 3e-7 relative, but the sharded gradients are exactly 8× too large. What is the bug, and why does the loss still match?
good_answer: Each device takes the mean loss over its local batch shard, and the gradients are summed (psum) over the data axis instead of averaged (pmean). That gives n× the gradient.
The logged loss can still match because it is averaged separately for logging, so loss parity alone does not prove gradient parity.
Fix: pmean the grads over the data axis inside shard_map, or compute the global mean loss under jit with NamedSharding inputs and let XLA insert the collective.
This is why the test compares every gradient leaf, not only the loss, and why an exact integer ratio points to an axis/reduction bug rather than numerics.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the per-leaf gradient comparison in the sharding test. Claude asks you to inject the psum bug and confirm the test catches it.

questions.q: Why can sharded and unsharded results not be bit-identical, and how do you pick a tolerance that still catches real bugs?
good_answer: Sharding changes the reduction order: sums are split into partial sums plus a collective, and floating-point addition is not associative.
In fp32 at highest precision on CPU, expect relative error around 1e-7 to 1e-5 on the loss and grads. In bf16 it would be ~1e-2.
Real bugs (a missing mean, the wrong spec or axis, a wrong mask) give errors of order 1 or exact integer factors, far above that.
Run the test in fp32 at highest matmul precision, and report max absolute and relative error per leaf, with a guard for leaves near zero.
questions.verify: Explain aloud. Claude gives three mismatch values and asks which are numerics and which are bugs.

questions.q: Design the <1 h TPU dry run. What must it prove for week 11, and why must it use the same slice type?

questions.q: On TPU, the parity check of your fp32 train step against the 4090 fails at ~1e-2 relative. What is the likely cause, and should training use the fix?

Set jax_default_matmul_precision to 'highest' on both sides for the parity test. The gap should drop to ~1e-6 to 1e-5.

questions.q: Could you tensor-parallel Qwen3-1.7B 8 ways or 16 ways? Check head counts, MLP width and vocab in the cached config.json against the mesh size, and say what you do when a dim does not divide.

weeks.title: Interpretability
weeks.theme: Week 10 uses the model you built to link a behavior change caused by training to something inside the network, and it closes the evidence for choosing the two capstone finalists.
goals: The NNX model returns a dict of per-layer residual activations and accepts an optional intervention, both as function arguments. A no-op intervention reproduces the plain forward, and changing the direction, strength or layer causes zero recompiles.
A contrastive set is built from your own runs (SFT→RL behavior change, or hacked vs honest samples from weeks 6 and 8), matched on prompt and length where possible, with item IDs saved.
A difference-of-means direction, plus per-layer linear probes with a Hewitt-Liang control task, reporting held-out selectivity per layer with splits made by prompt.

Ablating or adding the direction changes the target behavior, measured with paired CIs. The general-capability slice and a random-direction control are measured under the same intervention, and the layer is chosen on a separate split.
Base/SFT/DPO/RL are compared on identical token IDs, and ‖ΔW‖ (‖s·BA‖_F, absolute and relative) is plotted per layer and module for each adapter.
Friday: scorecard row 4 is filled with linked evidence, and the top-2 areas by weighted score are named as capstone finalists.
deliverables: Capture/intervention API with tests: the no-op intervention equals the plain forward, and there are zero new compiles across α, direction and layer sweeps.
Contrastive dataset with item IDs and a written check of confounds (length, format, padding position, surface tokens).
Per-layer probe accuracy and selectivity plot. Direction-intervention dose-response plot with a random-direction band and the capability curve.
One figure linking an internal change to a training-caused behavioral change across base/SFT/DPO/RL.
‖ΔW‖ per layer/module plot. Scorecard row 4 and the top-2 areas with their weighted totals.
learned: You can add activation capture and interventions to a jitted NNX model without hook frameworks or recompiles.
You can budget memory for activation capture and reduce on device before anything goes to the host.
You can derive directional ablation and steering, and explain how residual-norm growth in a pre-norm model changes their effect by layer.
You can run probes that control for memorization with a control task and prompt-level held-out splits.
You can design contrastive sets and controls so a direction reflects the behavior, not length, format or position.
You can compute and compare LoRA weight changes cheaply across modules of different shapes.
You can apply the statistics protocol to interventions across many layers, including multiple-comparison control and a separate split for picking the layer.

questions.q: Your forward takes intervene(layer, h) -> h. Why is passing a new Python function per experiment a recompile trap, and how do you structure the intervention so that sweeping direction, α and layer causes zero recompiles?
good_answer: Under jit a Python callable has to be static. A new function object, or a closure over new values, changes the cache key and retraces.
Use one fixed intervention whose parameters are traced arrays: direction [d_model], α as a scalar array, a per-layer weight or mask [n_layers], and a mode or ablation flag as an array.
Inside the layer loop (or scan), apply h + w[l]·α·d̂ or h − w[l]·(h·d̂)d̂, so every setting shares one compiled program. α must be a jnp array, not a Python float.
Proof: after warmup, sweep 5 α values and 3 layers with jax_log_compiles on and assert zero new compiles. Assert that α=0 (or w=0) equals the plain forward.
questions.verify: Show the pytest and the compile-count assertion, and run them.

questions.q: Capturing fp32 residual streams for all 28 layers of Qwen3-1.7B (d_model 2048) at B=32, T=512 costs how much memory? What do you store instead for 1,000 contrastive items?
good_answer: 28 × 32 × 512 × 2048 × 4 B ≈ 3.76 GB per batch, on top of weights and the forward pass.
Store one position per item (e.g. the last prompt token, or a mean over the response span under the mask): 28 × 1000 × 2048 × 4 B ≈ 229 MB.
Or capture only selected layers, or keep bf16 and upcast for analysis.
Reduce on device inside the jitted forward (gather the position or take the masked mean) so full [B, T, d] tensors never come back to the host.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the size of the saved activation file.

questions.q: Write the difference-of-means direction, the directional ablation and the steering update. Show that the ablated activation has zero projection on the direction, and explain why the same α has a different effect at different layers in a pre-norm model like Qwen3.
good_answer: d = μ_pos − μ_neg at the chosen layer and position, and d̂ = d/‖d‖.

Ablation: h′ = h − (h·d̂)d̂, so h′·d̂ = h·d̂ − (h·d̂)(d̂·d̂) = 0. Ablating at only one layer can be undone by later layers writing the direction back, so also try ablating at every layer and position.
Steering: h′ = h + αd̂.

In pre-norm residual models the residual norm usually grows with depth, and each block reads RMSNorm(h). A fixed α is therefore a smaller relative change at deep layers, so scale α to the typical ‖h‖ or to the std of h·d̂ at that layer.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the intervention code and its test that the projection after ablation is ~0.

questions.q: What is a Hewitt-Liang control task, how do you build one for your contrastive set, and what number do you report per layer?
good_answer: A control task gives labels the representation cannot encode as the real property: a random label fixed per prompt (or per token type), so only memorization can solve it.
Train the same probe architecture with the same regularization on the control task and on the real task, with train/test split by prompt.
Report selectivity = real-task held-out accuracy − control-task held-out accuracy, per layer.
High accuracy with low selectivity means the probe is expressive enough to memorize, not that the layer encodes the behavior.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the selectivity plot. Claude asks how you split train/test and what happens if the same prompt lands on both sides.

questions.q: The hacked-vs-honest probe reaches 98% held-out accuracy at layer 0. What is going on, and what checks do you run?
good_answer: Layer 0 is essentially token embeddings, so the label is readable from surface tokens: length, specific tokens (e.g. assert, test-file edits) or format.
Check the capture position. With right padding, index −1 is a pad token and leaks length. With left padding, check that the position is the intended token.
Match pairs on prompt and length, or capture on the prompt only (before the response), and rerun.
Compare with a bag-of-tokens baseline classifier. If it also gets ~98%, the probe is not evidence of an internal representation.
questions.verify: Explain aloud. Claude gives a per-layer probe curve and asks which check you run first.

questions.q: Design the contrastive set and the cross-model comparison for 'behavior changed by SFT→RL'. Why teacher-force identical token IDs through base/SFT/DPO/RL instead of letting each model generate?
good_answer: Use the same prompts. Positives are responses showing the RL-induced behavior, labeled by an automatic checker (e.g. the week-6 hacking signal or a format statistic). Negatives are matched responses (same prompt, similar length) without it.
Teacher-forcing identical token IDs makes the inputs identical across models, so activation differences come from the weights, not from different text.
If each model generates its own text, activation differences mix weight changes with changes in content, length and format.

Memory plan: one bf16 base plus adapters. SFT and DPO adapters sit on the base. The RL adapter sits on the merged-SFT base (a second ~3.4 GB copy, or apply the SFT and RL adapters unmerged), with the traced scale selecting each model.
questions.verify: Explain aloud. Claude probes the memory plan and the merged-base subtlety for the RL model.

questions.q: Ablating your direction at layer 18 drops the hacking rate from 30% to 12%. What controls and statistics do you need before claiming the direction mediates the behavior?
good_answer: Random-direction control: ablate many random unit vectors (e.g. 50) at the same layer and position to get a null distribution, ideally matched to the variance h·d̂ removes.
Measure the general-capability slice and MBPP dev pass@1 under the same ablation, to rule out a direction that just damages the model.
Paired bootstrap over items (the same items with and without ablation), with CIs, and compare the effect against the sampling-seed noise floor.
Testing 28 layers is far more than ~5 comparisons, so use a Holm correction or label per-layer results exploratory. Choose the layer on a separate split from the one you report.
Claim 'mediates' only as far as the evidence goes: necessity from ablation, and sufficiency only if adding the direction induces the behavior.
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the figure with the random-direction band. Claude checks which split chose the layer.

questions.q: How do you compute ‖ΔW‖_F for each LoRA adapter without forming the full d_out × d_in matrix, and how do you compare modules of different shapes (Qwen3-1.7B q_proj 2048×2048 vs down_proj 2048×6144)?
good_answer: ΔW = s · B A with B [d_out, r], A [r, d_in] and s = α/r (your traced scale).
‖BA‖_F² = tr(AᵀBᵀBA) = tr((BᵀB)(AAᵀ)), which needs only two r×r Gram matrices, so it is cheap.

Compare across modules with the relative change ‖ΔW‖_F / ‖W‖_F, not the raw norm, since bigger matrices have bigger norms. Optionally add the top singular values of ΔW (from the r×r core) to see whether the change is low-rank in practice.
For the RL adapter, W is the merged-SFT base, so the plot shows change relative to SFT, not to base. B is initialized at 0, so any nonzero norm is learned change.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then show the function and a pytest that it matches the norm of the explicitly formed product on a small module.

questions.q: Design the single headline figure that links an internal change to the training-caused behavior change. What goes on each axis, and what makes it more than a correlation?
good_answer: One option: for each checkpoint (base, SFT, DPO, RL, all seeds), plot the mean projection onto d̂ at the chosen layer, on identical teacher-forced inputs, against the behavior rate, with CIs.
Pair it with an intervention panel: behavior and capability vs α for ablation/steering, with the random-direction band, to show the causal direction.
Compute d̂ on a different split from the items plotted, so the figure is not circular.
State in the caption what it does not show (e.g. one direction among possibly many, one layer, one behavior metric) and link the command, config and per-item JSONL.
questions.verify: Sketch the figure on paper first, then show the generated plot. Claude plays a skeptical reviewer and asks what alternative explanation remains.

questions.q: You train an unregularized logistic probe on N=400 activations of dimension 2048 with random labels. Predict the train and held-out accuracy, and say what this means for your probe protocol.
good_answer: N points in general position in d dimensions are linearly separable for any labeling when N ≤ d+1 (Cover), so train accuracy is ~100%.
Held-out accuracy is ~50% (chance), because there is no signal.
So train accuracy means nothing here. Report held-out accuracy with prompt-level splits, use L2 regularization chosen on a validation split, or reduce dimension (PCA) or increase N.
The control task makes the same point per layer.
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then run the random-label probe and compare.

questions.q: Sweep steering α from 0 up to 4× the typical projection magnitude at a layer. Predict the shape of the target-behavior curve and the capability curve, and say how you choose the α you report.
good_answer: Target behavior rises roughly monotonically at small α, then saturates or becomes erratic.

questions.q: Predict the ideal decode time per step and tokens/s for Qwen3-1.7B in bf16 on the 4090 at batch 1 with a short context. Then predict the same at batch 64 with 1024 cached tokens per sequence.
good_answer: Params from config.json (d=2048, 28 layers, 16 Q heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, d_ff 6144, vocab 151936, tied): attention q 2048x2048 + k,v 2048x1024 each + o 2048x2048 = about 12.6M per layer, MLP 3x2048x6144 = about 37.7M, so about 50.3M x 28 = 1.41B, plus 151936x2048 = 311M embedding, about 1.72B total, about 3.44 GB in bf16
The tied embedding is read in full as the lm_head every step, so batch 1 reads about 3.44 GB: at about 1.0 TB/s that is about 3.4 ms/step, about 290 tokens/s upper bound
KV per token = 28 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 x 2 (K and V) x 2 bytes = 114,688 B, about 112 KiB

Batch 64 x 1024 tokens = 65,536 tokens x 112 KiB, about 7.5 GB of KV read per step, plus 3.44 GB of weights, about 11 GB, about 11 ms/step, so about 64/0.011, about 5,800 tokens/s ideal (and falling as generated tokens grow the cache)
Measured numbers well below the ideal (for example under 60-80%) point to overhead such as Python dispatch, unfused ops, KV cache copies or recompiles, not physics
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the roofline column in the inference table; Claude checks the arithmetic against the model's config.json in the repo

questions.q: Using arithmetic intensity, explain why decode at batch 1 is memory-bound and at which batch size (ignoring KV) it would become compute-bound on the 4090. Then explain why attention over the KV cache stays memory-bound no matter how large the batch is.
good_answer: The weight matmuls in decode do about 2N FLOPs per token and read about 2N bytes of bf16 weights once per step, shared across the batch, so intensity is about B FLOPs/byte at batch B
The 4090 ridge point is peak dense bf16 tensor FLOPs (about 165 TFLOPS with fp32 accumulate) over about 1.0 TB/s, about 165 FLOPs/byte, so weights alone would need batch about 150-170

Each sequence has its own KV cache, so batching does not reuse KV bytes: per cached token and KV head, K is 256 bytes and the QK dot for the g query heads sharing it is about 2 x 128 x g FLOPs, so intensity is about g FLOPs/byte, and the same holds for V
With GQA g = 16/8 = 2, so attention runs at about 2 FLOPs/byte, far below 165: GQA cuts KV bytes, but it does not change the regime
questions.verify: Explain aloud; Claude probes with follow-ups such as what the ridge point and batch threshold become on an H100 SXM at about 3.35 TB/s

questions.q: Suppose your TTFT is about 3 s at batch 64, prompt 1024 and about 6 ms at batch 1, prompt 128. Show that both numbers are plausible, say which resource bounds each, and name the implementation detail that would make the large case run out of memory.
good_answer: Prefill FLOPs are about 2 x N x prompt tokens: batch 1 x 128 is about 2 x 1.72e9 x 128, about 0.44 TFLOP (about 2.7 ms at peak), while 64 x 1024 = 65,536 tokens is about 190-225 TFLOP depending on whether the lm_head runs on every position
Batch 1 x 128 has intensity about 128 FLOPs/byte, just under the ridge, so the 3.44 GB weight read (about 3.4 ms) and the compute (about 2.7 ms) are comparable: about 6 ms with overhead is plausible
Batch 64 x 1024 is compute-bound: at about 165 TFLOPS and 40-50% utilization it takes about 2.3-3 s; causal attention adds about 4 x 28 x 2048 x 512 FLOPs per token, under 5% at this length
Computing the lm_head on every prompt position would make [65536, 151936] logits, about 20 GB in bf16, so prefill must take only the last position's hidden state before the lm_head
TTFT and inter-token latency sit in different regimes, so they must be reported separately
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the TTFT column; Claude asks what MFU your measured prefill implies

questions.q: With preallocation on, nvidia-smi shows about 18 GB in use for every cell of your table. How do you fill the memory column and the measured memory table so they mean something?
good_answer: By default JAX preallocates about 75% of GPU memory (XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION), so nvidia-smi shows the pool, not what is used

Use jitted_fn.lower(...).compile().memory_analysis() for argument, output, temp and generated-code bytes per compiled function (verify field names), and jax.devices()[0].memory_stats()['peak_bytes_in_use'] after a run for the real peak

Compare each component with the arithmetic: weights 3.44 GB, KV = B x max_len x 112 KiB (for example 64 x 2048 tokens is about 15 GB), and activations/temp from memory_analysis, then explain any gap, such as a second KV copy because donation is missing
Optionally take a jax.profiler device memory profile to attribute large buffers; never turn preallocation off to make nvidia-smi readable, because that changes the latency being benchmarked
questions.verify: Show the memory table next to the week-3 arithmetic and the code that reads memory_analysis and memory_stats; Claude asks you to explain the largest discrepancy

questions.q: Design the benchmark protocol for the sampler-vs-vLLM table so that a reviewer cannot dismiss it. Which knobs must be fixed or logged, how are TTFT and inter-token latency defined, and how do you prove nothing recompiled during the timed region?
good_answer: Same weights and dtype, same chat template, same prompt token IDs, fixed output length (ignore EOS or force max_new_tokens on both sides), same temperature and top-p
Definitions: TTFT = time from request to first token, including prefill; inter-token latency = (total time - TTFT) / (output tokens - 1); throughput = total output tokens / wall time for the batch

Warmup and compile excluded, jax.block_until_ready on the outputs before stopping the clock, median and p90 over at least 10 runs, GPU idle otherwise (check nvidia-smi), with clocks and power limit logged
JAX preallocation on; vLLM gpu_memory_utilization and version logged, vLLM run in a separate process at a different time so the two never share the GPU

Zero recompiles: every grid shape is pre-warmed into its bucket and jax_log_compiles is enabled, so any compile line inside the timed loop fails the run; the results row logs git SHA, config hash, sampler version, allocator settings, accelerator and the per-run JSONL path
