questions.q: You quantize all linear layers of Qwen3-1.7B to int8 with per-output-channel scales. Predict the ideal speedup at batch 1, and at batch 64 with 1024 cached tokens. What changes if you leave the tied lm_head in bf16?
good_answer: Batch 1, everything int8 including the tied embedding/lm_head: about 1.72 GB plus small scales, so about 1.7 ms vs 3.4 ms, about 2x ideal
lm_head kept bf16: 1.41 GB int8 + 0.62 GB bf16, about 2.03 GB, so 3.44/2.03, about 1.7x
Batch 64 x 1024: the KV of about 7.5 GB is unchanged, so (3.44 + 7.5) / (1.72 + 7.5), about 1.19x: weight-only quantization helps small, weight-bound batches, not KV-bound large ones
For W of shape [in, out], per-output-channel scale s_j = max_i |W_ij| / 127 and W_q = round(W / s); y = (x @ W_q) * s can apply the scale after the dot because it is constant along each output column
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the bytes/step vs latency table; Claude checks which tensors you actually quantized in the code

questions.q: Int8 shows about 0% speedup over bf16 at batch 1. Walk through how you diagnose it in the optimized HLO and the profiler trace, and what each finding means.
good_answer: Dump the optimized HLO with jax.jit(f).lower(...).compile().as_text() and look at what feeds each dot: a cuBLAS gemm custom-call or a Triton gemm fusion

Unfused: a separate fusion converts s8[in,out] to bf16[in,out] (sometimes times the scale) and writes a full bf16 weight to HBM, then a cuBLAS gemm reads it, so each step moves more bytes than plain bf16
Fused: the convert sits inside the same fusion as the dot (for example a Triton gemm fusion with an s8 operand), and the trace shows one kernel per matmul with no extra weight-sized write

Fixes: apply the scale after the dot, check the XLA GPU Triton gemm flags for your JAX version, write a Pallas int8 x bf16 kernel (Triton lowering on sm_89), or compare against Qwix (verify API); then re-measure bytes/step against the roofline
questions.verify: Point to the HLO lines and the trace kernels on screen; Claude asks you to predict the number of kernels per layer before you open the trace

questions.q: How do you decide whether int8 changed MBPP accuracy under the statistics protocol? Which test applies, which does not, and what does 'no degradation' have to mean?
good_answer: Same frozen test IDs, same sampler, same chat template and decoding config, and per-item comparison of bf16 against int8

For per-item pass rates from n samples (for example n=16 at T=0.7), use the paired bootstrap over items (harness/stats.py paired_bootstrap) or Wilcoxon signed-rank; McNemar only fits single-sample greedy pass@1
There is no training seed, so this is a one-level paired bootstrap over items, with each item's pass rate pooled over sampling seeds; compare the delta with the noise floor (SD over 3 sampling seeds)

Pre-commit an equivalence margin (for example plus or minus 2 pts): claim no degradation only if the whole paired 95% CI falls inside it, not because the point estimate is small or the CI contains 0; report the HumanEval+ OOD delta the same way
questions.verify: Show the result row and the paired_bootstrap call from harness/stats.py; Claude asks why McNemar would be wrong here and what your margin was

questions.q: Write the MFU formula you use and compute MFU for a 200M model with d_model=1024, 16 layers, sequence 1024, running at 400k tokens/s on v5e-8 (about 197 TFLOPS bf16 per chip). How wrong is the number if you drop the attention term, and what should N include?
good_answer: MFU = (FLOPs per token x tokens/s) / (chips x peak bf16 FLOPs), with FLOPs per token = 6N + 12 x L x d x T (the PaLM attention term, with d = heads x head_dim and T = sequence length)
6N = 1.2e9 and 12 x 16 x 1024 x 1024 is about 2.0e8, so about 1.4e9 FLOPs per token
1.4e9 x 4e5 = 5.6e14 FLOP/s over 8 x 1.97e14 = 1.58e15 is about 35% MFU; with 6N only it is about 30%, an underestimate of about 14%
N counts every matmul weight, including the output vocab projection (V x d costs real FLOPs even when tied), but not the embedding lookup; state the choice and keep it fixed across the curve
Remat recompute is not counted (counting it gives HFU, not MFU), and peak is the per-chip dense bf16 spec for the exact chip (v6e is much higher, verify)
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then point to the MFU function in your code and recompute one point of the plotted curve with Claude

questions.q: Going from 1 to 8 chips, DP MFU drops from 45% to 30%. Is that strong or weak scaling, what are the likely causes, and what single experiment separates them?
good_answer: Say first whether the global batch was fixed (strong scaling: per-chip batch shrinks by 8x) or the per-chip batch was fixed (weak scaling); the curve means different things in each case
Strong scaling: smaller per-chip matmuls run less efficiently and the gradient all-reduce stays the same size while compute per chip shrinks, so the communication fraction rises
Weak scaling: compute per chip is constant, so a drop points to all-reduce time not overlapped with the backward pass, or to host-side input or dispatch stalls

Experiment: in the profiler trace, measure collective time and whether it overlaps compute, then rerun 8 chips at the same per-chip batch as 1 chip; if MFU recovers it was per-chip work size, and if not it is communication or input
questions.verify: Show the trace with the all-reduce region annotated and the two curves; Claude asks you to predict the communication fraction before opening the trace

questions.q: Your FSDP run on 8 chips shows per-chip memory equal to the 1-chip run and tokens/s barely above 1 chip. Name the likely bugs and how you would confirm each in the HLO, with array.sharding, or with memory_stats.
good_answer: Params and optimizer state created replicated: the variables have no sharding metadata (nnx.with_partitioning or sharding names), or the model and optimizer were not built inside a jitted init that applies jax.lax.with_sharding_constraint with nnx.get_partition_spec(nnx.state(model)), so Adam m and v sit fully on every chip
Batch not sharded on the data axis: every chip computes the same full batch, so throughput does not scale and the HLO may show no gradient collective at all
Train step outputs come back replicated because out_shardings or donation do not match the input shardings, so params get resharded or copied every step

Confirm with print(x.sharding) or jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding on 1D/2D leaves, per-device memory_stats, and a grep of the compiled HLO: correct FSDP shows all-gathers of 1/8 param shards and reduce-scatters of grads, not a full-size all-reduce or none
questions.verify: Show the HLO grep, the sharding printout and memory_stats before and after the fix; Claude asks which collective you expected for each parameter

questions.q: For Megatron-style TP on one layer's MLP, which weight do you shard on which axis, and where must a collective appear in your shard_map version? Why does TP stop paying off from 2 to 8 chips for a 200M model?
good_answer: Up and gate projections sharded column-wise (PartitionSpec(None, 'model')), down projection row-wise (PartitionSpec('model', None)), so SiLU and the elementwise product stay local to each shard

In shard_map one psum over 'model' goes after the down projection in forward; autodiff of shard_map adds the matching all-reduce on the input gradient in backward, so Megatron uses 2 all-reduces per layer in forward (attention and MLP) and 2 in backward
Each all-reduce moves about B_local x T x d activations and does not shrink as the TP degree grows, while each chip's matmul shrinks to d x d_ff/n, so the communication-to-compute ratio grows with n
So at 100-300M, DP or FSDP should win on MFU, and TP is there to learn the mechanism; TP pays off when weights or activations do not fit per chip, or the per-chip batch would otherwise be too small
questions.verify: Show the shard_map layer (check whether your JAX uses jax.shard_map or jax.experimental.shard_map) and its parity test against the auto-sharded version; Claude probes where the backward collective appears in the HLO

questions.q: Draft the compute plan for one capstone pre-registration using this week's measured numbers. What must the note contain, and how do you check it fits the budget?

Seeds: 5 for the capstone headline and 3 for its ablation arm, so the run count is (5 + 3) x configs, with the eval cost (for example n=16 on test + OOD) counted as well

questions.q: Stretch: speculative decoding with Qwen3-0.6B drafting for Qwen3-1.7B. With per-token acceptance rate alpha and k draft tokens, what is the expected number of tokens per verify step, and when is it a net loss on the 4090 at batch 1?
good_answer: Expected tokens per target pass = (1 - alpha^(k+1)) / (1 - alpha); with alpha=0.7 and k=4 that is about 2.8
Cost per round is about k draft steps plus one target verify pass over k+1 tokens; at batch 1 the verify pass costs about one target decode step because it is memory-bound

Bandwidth-only, the draft (about 1.2 GB bf16) costs about 0.35 of a target step, giving a round cost of about 1 + 0.35 x 4 = 2.4 and about 1.15x speedup; but Qwen3-0.6B also has 28 layers, so per-step dispatch overhead is similar and the real draft cost ratio is likely higher, which shrinks the gain

Net loss when alpha is low or k is too large, and the gain shrinks at large batch once verification stops being nearly free; both models share the tokenizer, and the rejection-sampling acceptance rule keeps the output distribution exactly the target's
questions.verify: Derive on paper; if implemented, compare against the measured accepted tokens per round and latency from your sampler logs

questions.q: Predict the largest rollout batch for Qwen3-4B (36 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, ~4.0B params, tied embeddings) in bf16 on the 24 GiB 4090 at 1024 total tokens per sequence. Do it first with JAX's default preallocation fraction, then with XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.9.
good_answer: Weights: ~4.0e9 x 2 B = ~8.0 GB = ~7.5 GiB, with one copy only because embeddings are tied
KV per token = 2 (K,V) x 36 x 8 x 128 x 2 B = 147,456 B = 144 KiB, so 144 MiB per 1024-token sequence; batch 64 = 9.0 GiB, batch 128 = 18 GiB

Default fraction 0.75 gives ~18 GiB, leaving ~10.5 GiB after weights. Batch 64 (9 GiB) fits with ~1.5 GiB for prefill activations, last-position logits and workspace, so it is tight. Batch ~48 is the safe choice
At 0.9 (~21.6 GiB) there is ~14 GiB of headroom. Batch 64 fits comfortably, ~80-96 is the ceiling, and 128 (18 GiB) does not fit

Caveats: the env var must be set before `import jax`; the KV cache must be updated in place (inside while_loop or donated), otherwise peak memory doubles; prefill must not materialize [B, T, V] logits
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then run the teacher sampler at batch 64, 96 and 128 with the fraction at 0.9 and compare against `compile().memory_analysis()` or the profiler peak; Claude checks the arithmetic

questions.q: You switch the teacher to Gemma 3 4B. Your strict loader raises unmapped `vision_tower.*` and `multi_modal_projector.*` keys and missing `model.layers.0.*` keys. A teammate suggests making the loader lenient. What is going on, what is the right fix, and what breaks with the lenient route?
good_answer: The checkpoint is multimodal: language weights sit under a `language_model.` prefix (check the exact prefix in model.safetensors.index.json), next to vision tower and projector weights

Fix: strip the language-model prefix explicitly and keep an explicit skip list for the vision and projector keys. Still error on any other unmapped or missing key, and read tie_word_embeddings from the config (Gemma 3 and Qwen3 up to 4B tie, so there is no lm_head tensor)
A lenient loader would leave every layer, or lm_head, at its random init. The code runs and produces fluent-looking garbage, and nothing crashes
Logit parity against the HF text-only forward catches this at once: the max abs diff is O(1-10), not ~1e-3 at `highest`
Gemma-specific parity traps: embedding scaling by sqrt(d_model), RMSNorm with (1 + w), QK-norm, 5:1 local/global sliding-window attention, and a 262k vocab that needs chunked log-probs
questions.verify: Show the loader's prefix and skip lists and the parity pytest; Claude renames one layer's key in a copy of the index and asks you to show the error

questions.q: Design the three arms (random, difficulty-filtered, failure-targeted) at a fixed 1k budget. State exactly what is held fixed, where the difficulty signal comes from, and which confound is most likely to explain a win by the failure-targeted arm.
good_answer: Held fixed: teacher, pool, verifier and filters, chat template, LoRA config, LR, steps or epochs, seeds and eval protocol. The budget is 1k examples, and tokens per arm are reported (or the budget is matched on tokens, if that was pre-registered)
Difficulty signal: the student's pass rate (base or SFT checkpoint, pre-registered) from n samples (e.g. 16) on train prompts only, computed before selection and then frozen

Random draws uniformly from the verified pool. Difficulty-filtered takes prompts with intermediate student pass rate (e.g. 0 < p < 0.5). Failure-targeted takes prompts with student p = 0 that the teacher solves
Main confound: harder prompts produce longer solutions, so failure-targeted gets more tokens and gradient signal per example. Report tokens per arm or add a token-matched control
Secondary confounds: fewer distinct prompts with more near-duplicate solutions each, and a shift in problem types away from the test distribution
questions.verify: Explain aloud; Claude proposes an alternative explanation for a result and asks which control rules it out

questions.q: data/splits.json leaves 274 MBPP train prompts (100 went to dev). Suppose the student solves none of its 16 samples on 30% of them, and the teacher solves half of those. How many distinct prompts can the failure-targeted arm draw from, how many solutions per prompt does a 1k budget imply, and what do you do about it?
good_answer: 274 x 0.3 x 0.5 = ~41 prompts
1000 / 41 = ~24 verified solutions per prompt, many near-identical. Even the random arm averages ~3.6 per prompt
The arm will overfit a narrow set of problems, so any win or loss partly measures prompt diversity rather than targeting
Options (pre-register one): dedup by normalized text or AST and cap solutions per prompt; add decontaminated APPS-introductory prompts to the pool for all arms; or lower the budget for all arms
Log the distinct-prompt count and the per-prompt cap for every arm in the table
questions.verify: Count prompts with student p=0 and a teacher solve in your own pool JSONL and compare with the prediction

questions.q: Explain how your 13-gram decontamination works on code: what you normalize and tokenize, what you check against, which false positives you expect, and what it cannot catch.
good_answer: Normalize (strip comments and docstrings, collapse whitespace), tokenize in one fixed way (whitespace or the model tokenizer), and build 13-gram sets from the prompts, reference solutions and tests of MBPP test, MBPP+, HumanEval+ and dev
Flag a pool example if it shares any 13-gram, or more than a set overlap fraction, with an eval item. Report hits per arm, because arms can differ in contamination
False positives: boilerplate and common idioms (e.g. `if __name__ == "__main__":`, standard loops) collide, so use a whitelist or a minimum overlap fraction
Misses: paraphrased problems, renamed variables and different but equivalent solutions. It also cannot detect that the teacher memorized MBPP or HumanEval during pretraining
Also run it on the train prompts themselves against test, because MBPP may contain near-duplicate tasks across splits (verify)
questions.verify: Plant one verbatim test solution and one with renamed variables in a toy pool, run the decontamination script, and show which one is caught

questions.q: Your table compares 3 arms pairwise on 3 eval sets, giving these sorted two-sided bootstrap p-values: 0.004, 0.011, 0.02, 0.03, 0.04, 0.12, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7. Apply Holm at alpha = 0.05. Which are significant, and how should the week have been set up instead?
good_answer: m = 3 pairs x 3 sets = 9 comparisons, more than ~5, so protocol 3.2 rule 7 requires Holm or an exploratory label
Holm compares p_(i) (i = 1..m, ascending) with alpha / (m - i + 1): 0.004 < 0.05/9 = 0.0056 passes; 0.011 > 0.05/8 = 0.00625 fails, so stop. Only the first comparison is significant
Uncorrected, five comparisons would have looked significant, which is how forking paths inflate claims
Better: pre-register 1-2 primary contrasts (e.g. failure-targeted vs random on MBPP test) and label the rest secondary or exploratory
p-value from the two-level bootstrap: ~2 x min(fraction of replicates <= 0, fraction >= 0). McNemar is invalid here because per-item outcomes are pass rates from 16 samples
questions.verify: Compute by hand, then write or point to a Holm helper in harness/stats.py with a pytest on these numbers; Claude checks the thresholds

questions.q: Write the selection function for the failure-targeted arm. It takes the student per-item JSONL and the verified teacher pool and returns exactly 1k example IDs. Which pytests must it pass?
good_answer: Deterministic given a seed (an explicit numpy Generator, no global state): same inputs and seed give the same IDs
Asserts that every prompt ID is in splits.json['train'], with none from dev, test or OOD
Asserts the budget is exactly 1000 and that every example passed the verifier, plus any extra filter that the pre-registration applies to all arms
Enforces the per-prompt cap and the dedup rule, and logs distinct prompts and total tokens
Raises if the pool cannot fill the budget, instead of silently returning fewer examples
questions.verify: Show and run the pytest file; Claude asks you to break one invariant and confirm a test fails

questions.q: Many teacher generations hit the token cap and the verified rate is far below what you expected. Students trained on the pool also emit stray `<think>` tags at eval. What happened, and how do you fix it?
good_answer: The teacher was rendered with the Qwen3 template's default thinking mode, so it wrote long `<think>` blocks that were truncated before the code and then failed verification
The students learned the teacher's format, which does not match the eval prompt; extract_code strips think blocks, but truncated or malformed outputs still fail
Fix: render with enable_thinking=False (an empty think block after the generation prompt) in teacher generation, SFT formatting and eval, as harness/prompts.py documents
Build each SFT example as the exact eval prompt tokens (add_generation_prompt, thinking off) plus the completion tokens, and test that its prefix token IDs equal the eval prompt's
Log the template and decoding config in every results row
questions.verify: Show the rendered token IDs for one item in all three paths; Claude compares them

questions.q: Some teacher solutions pass MBPP's 3 base tests but would fail stricter tests. Only 55 of the 274 train prompts have a plus-compatible MBPP+ test (splits.json['plus_compatible']). Should weak-test-only solutions be in the pool, and how do you keep the ablation fair?
good_answer: They may be partly wrong programs. Training on them teaches the student to pass weak tests, a data-level version of the verifier gap from week 6
The stricter filter only applies to the ~20% of train prompts with compatible plus tests. Filtering just those changes the prompt mix unevenly, and hard prompts may be over- or under-represented
Measure the plus-fail fraction per arm on the 55 covered prompts. If it differs across arms it is a confound, so apply the same rule to all arms (or none) and pre-register it
Never use plus tests of test or dev items for filtering; the held-out verifier must stay held out
questions.verify: Compute the per-arm fraction from the pool JSONL, restricted to plus_compatible train IDs; Claude probes whether the filter leaks test information

questions.q: Before the pilot, predict how long one data-ablation SFT run and its eval take on the 4090, and decide whether the ablation needs a cloud burst. Use ~400 tokens per example, 3 epochs, and the week-0 measurement of ~215 generated tokens per completion.
good_answer: Training tokens: 1000 x 400 x 3 = 1.2M

LoRA with remat costs ~6N FLOPs per token: 2N forward, ~2N for activation grads (no base weight grads), ~2N recompute. 6 x 1.7e9 x 1.2e6 = ~1.2e16 FLOPs, ~3 min at ~40% of 165 TFLOPs; small batches make it ~5-10 min in practice

Eval: 500 x 16 x ~215 = ~1.7M tokens on MBPP test (MBPP+ re-verifies the same samples) plus 163 x 16 on HumanEval+. At a few thousand tok/s with your sampler that is ~10 min, plus the CPU verifier (~10k samples at <1 s each across workers)
9 checkpoints x ~20-25 min = ~3-4 h, so the whole ablation fits locally overnight and burst trigger 3.4(a) does not apply
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with the measured step time and eval time in the results rows

questions.q: After row 6 the weighted totals (max 65) are 47 for RLVR and 44 for synthetic data. Do you run one pilot or two, and what must each pilot measure so that Friday's launch is copy-paste?
good_answer: (47 - 44) / 47 = 6.4% < 10%, so you run one pilot per finalist and choose the capstone from the pilot evidence (selection rule 3)
Each pilot uses the same hardware type, JAX pin, config and launch.sh as the full run: a short run (20-50 steps) plus the full eval path

It measures steady-state step time (excluding compile), extrapolated hours per run, peak memory, rollout tokens/s, eval time, cost per run, a kill-and-resume on spot, and whether the compilation cache and Orbax uploads to the bucket work
It checks that early curves match a local run of the same config within noise
Update the compute plan (runs x measured hours x price) against the $150 reservation, and commit it before launch
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then show the pilot log(s) and the compute-plan diff in the pre-registration commit

weeks.exit_check: You are done with this week when the decontaminated data ablation table (3 arms x 3 seeds, two-level paired CIs, tokens and distinct prompts per arm) is committed, scorecard row 6 and the final pre-registration are committed, and the capstone runs are running on the cloud config with pilot-measured hours.
pitfalls: Generating the pool before parity passes, so the teacher has silently unloaded or misnamed weights
Letting the arms differ in tokens, distinct prompts or filtering rules, then crediting the selection strategy for the difference
Using any dev, test or MBPP+ test-item information in the difficulty signal or the filters
Spending Thursday-Friday on more ablation seeds instead of the pilot, which pushes the capstone launch into week 13

weeks.title: Capstone run + decision
weeks.theme: This week produces the plan's deciding evidence: a pre-registered, 5-seed capstone on an existing pipeline, written up as public post #3 and turned into a one-page area decision.
goals: Mon-Wed: finish the capstone runs (headline 2 arms x 5 seeds, ablation arm x 3 seeds) within the reserved $150, recover spot preemptions via Orbax resume, keep seeds balanced across hardware, and follow the pre-registered exclusion rules

Evaluate every final checkpoint with the frozen protocol: MBPP test (500), MBPP+ on the 165 plus-compatible test items, HumanEval+ OOD (163), the general-capability slice, and unbiased pass@k with n >= 2k (n=64 on the 200-item subset for high k, if pre-registered)

Analyze the headline with the two-level paired bootstrap, per-seed paired differences and the three-part headline rule (gain > 2x noise floor, CI excludes 0, same sign on every seed), and state the MDE next to the result
Thu-Fri: publish post #3 (question, related work, setup, results with two-level CIs, ablation, failures, next steps), with every number linked to its command and config
Write the one-page decision memo following the 5-step decision rule: capstone as the deciding row, Surprise >= 4 from your own data, the dropped area and why, 3 follow-ups with compute plans
Delete all cloud instances the same day, and close the cost ledger
deliverables: Per-item JSONL for every capstone checkpoint, with full results rows (SHA, config hash, template, decoding, sampler version, seeds, allocator, accelerator, accelerator_hours, cost_usd)
Capstone results table and figures: per-seed curves plus mean, two-level CIs, per-seed paired differences, pass@k curves with CIs at every k, and the MBPP vs MBPP+ gap
Public post #3 (capstone report) in the repo README, with reproducible commands
One-page decision memo: chosen area, scorecard with the capstone row, the dropped area and why, and 3 follow-up experiments with compute plans that fit the compute rule
Final cost ledger in the README (cost per run and running total against the ~$400 planned bound)
learned: You can run a multi-seed, multi-arm cloud experiment to a pre-registered plan, including preemption recovery and hardware balancing, without changing the plan after seeing results
You can compute and explain a two-level paired bootstrap, its weaknesses at 5 seeds, and what the sign rule adds
You can predict the capstone's CI width and minimum detectable effect from seed and item variance before reading the result
You can tell an underpowered null from evidence against an effect of the predicted size, and write a decision that holds up either way
You can write a research report where every number is reproducible from a committed command and config
You can make and defend an area decision from your own evidence, including the case where the capstone falsifies the leader

questions.q: Under a null where each seed's paired difference is equally likely to be positive or negative, what is the chance that all 5 headline seeds share a sign? What about 3 seeds? What does this say about the sign rule?
good_answer: On its own the sign rule is a weak test at 3 seeds and moderate at 5. It is a consistency check that complements the CI, not a significance test
It catches a pooled CI that excludes 0 only because one seed has a large effect while others go the other way
If seeds share data order or hardware quirks they are positively correlated, and the chance of a shared sign under the null is higher than these numbers
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then explain aloud; Claude asks how the answer changes if seeds are not independent

questions.q: Predict the 95% CI half-width of the headline difference before you see results. Assume a per-arm seed SD of 2 pts and a per-item paired-difference SD of 0.25 in pass rate over 500 items. Compare 5 seeds with 3 seeds and state the MDE.
good_answer: Seed term: sqrt(2^2/5 + 2^2/5) = sqrt(1.6) = ~1.26 pts
Total SE = sqrt(1.26^2 + 1.1^2) = ~1.68 pts, so the half-width is ~1.96 x 1.68 = ~3.3 pts
With 3 seeds the seed term is sqrt(8/3) = ~1.63, the total is ~1.98, and the half-width is ~3.9 pts

MDE at 80% power, 5% two-sided, is ~2.8 x SE = ~4.7 pts with 5 seeds, and somewhat larger in practice because seed SD estimated from 5 seeds is noisy (t with few df). A smaller predicted effect cannot be confirmed
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then plug in the measured seed SD and item SD from your capstone JSONL and compare with the bootstrap CI

questions.q: Check the capstone compute plan: 13 runs, a pilot measurement of 2.5 h per run on an H100 SXM, and ~$2.5/h spot. Does it fit the $150 reservation, and what do you cut first if run time and price are both 50% higher?
good_answer: 13 x 2.5 h = 32.5 GPU-h, ~$81. With cloud eval and ~20% margin it is ~$100, which fits
At +50% on both: 13 x 3.75 h x $3.75/h = ~$183, which is over budget
Protect the 5 headline seeds. Cut the ablation arm to 2 seeds labeled exploratory, move eval to the 4090 overnight, or run some seeds of both arms on the 4090 with matched assignment
Never spend past the hard cap. Log cost_usd and accelerator_hours per row and delete instances the same day
questions.verify: Show the compute-plan section of the pre-registration and the actual cost ledger; Claude checks the arithmetic

questions.q: A spot preemption killed headline seed 3 at step 140. After resume, reward jumps and KL to the reference spikes for ~10 steps. List the likely causes in order and the test that would have caught them.
good_answer: Adam moments not restored (zeros) while the step count was kept: bias correction is ~1, so the update m_hat/sqrt(v_hat) is ~(1-b1)g/sqrt(1-b2)|g|, about 3 x sign(g), much larger than a trained Adam step
The step counter or LR schedule reset, replaying warmup or jumping to a different LR
The reference changed: the merged SFT weights were not restored as before, or the reference was not run with the RL adapter at traced scale 0
PRNG keys not derived via fold_in(step), so post-resume rollouts differ; this adds noise but not a systematic spike
Test: kill at step k, resume, and assert that the loss and LoRA params at step k+1 match an uninterrupted run (exactly, or to bf16 tolerance)
questions.verify: Show the kill-and-resume pytest or the week-4/5 dry-run log; Claude asks which checkpointed items are optional

questions.q: Seed 4 of the treatment arm diverged and was killed by your early-kill criterion. Can you replace it with seed 6, drop it, or keep it? What goes in the report?
good_answer: Follow the exclusion rule committed in the pre-registration before launch. If it says killed runs are replaced by the next seed, run seed 6 and report the kill. If not, the seed stays in at its last checkpoint or is scored as a failure
Dropping it after seeing results is post-hoc selection and biases the headline toward the less stable arm
Report the divergence rate per arm as a result: an intervention that diverges more often is worse even if the surviving seeds score higher
Show with- and without-run views only if both were pre-registered; otherwise label the second one exploratory
questions.verify: Explain aloud, then point to the exclusion rule in the pre-registration commit; Claude checks that it predates the launch

questions.q: Two seeds of each arm ran on the 4090 and three on rented H100s. Is it valid to combine them? Design the assignment that keeps the comparison clean.
good_answer: The same JAX pin and config still give different numerics across devices: XLA autotuning picks different kernels and bf16 reductions are not associative, so trajectories diverge early
Hardware is acceptable as seed-like noise only if balanced: seed i of both arms runs on the same hardware type
Never run all of arm A on one device type and all of arm B on another; that confounds hardware with treatment
Log the accelerator in every results row and check that per-seed paired differences do not cluster by hardware
questions.verify: Show the results rows with the accelerator field, then the per-seed differences split by hardware; Claude asks what you would conclude if they clustered

questions.q: The headline CI is [-1.2, +3.8] pts and the pre-registered predicted effect was +6 pts. Is this a null result, a falsification, or underpowered? How does the decision memo handle it?
good_answer: The CI includes 0, so the headline claim fails
The upper bound of 3.8 is below the predicted +6, so the data are evidence against an effect of the predicted size. That is informative, not merely underpowered
If the leader's premise depended on a ~6 pt effect, decision rule step 4 allows choosing the runner-up, citing the week-12 pilot evidence
The memo states the MDE, enters the capstone as the deciding row, checks that the chosen area still has a Surprise >= 4 row, and names a follow-up that fits the compute rule
questions.verify: Explain aloud; Claude changes the CI (e.g. to [-1, +9]) and asks how the conclusion changes

questions.q: If your pre-registration includes a 4B scale check (Qwen3-4B, LoRA rank 16 on all linear layers, on one 32 GB v6e chip), estimate the LoRA parameter count, optimizer memory, base weights, rollout KV at batch 64 x 1024 and remat activations for an 8 x 1024 microbatch. Does it fit?
good_answer: Per layer r x (d_in + d_out) with d=2560, q_out=4096, kv_out=1024, ffn=9728: q and o 106,496 each, k and v 57,344 each, gate, up and down 196,608 each, ~917k total; x36 = ~33M params
fp32 param + grad + Adam m and v = 16 B/param, ~0.53 GB
Base weights in bf16 are ~8 GB. The reference is the same weights at adapter scale 0, so there is no second copy
Rollout KV: 64 x 1024 x 144 KiB = 9 GiB. Remat at layer boundaries: 8 x 1024 x 2560 x 2 B = ~42 MB x 36 = ~1.5 GB, plus one layer's recompute working set

Full fp32 logits would be 8 x 1024 x 151,936 x 4 B = ~5 GB, so use chunked log-probs. Total ~20 GB fits in 32 GB if the rollout and training peaks do not coexist (free or donate the KV cache before the train step)
questions.verify: Derive on paper, then compare with `compile().memory_analysis()` or a profiler memory trace from the scale-check run

questions.q: The headline improves MBPP test by 5 pts with a clean CI, but HumanEval+ is flat and the MBPP vs MBPP+ gap on the 165 plus-compatible items widened. How do you interpret this, and how does it change the claim in post #3?
good_answer: A widened base-vs-stricter gap means part of the gain comes from passing weak tests rather than writing correct code, the reward-hacking signature from week 6
Flat OOD means the gain does not transfer beyond the MBPP distribution
Report the gap change with its own two-level paired CI on the plus-compatible subset, then inspect ~30 samples that pass MBPP and fail MBPP+ and categorize them
Narrow the claim to what holds on MBPP+, and list the gap as a failure mode and a next step
questions.verify: Compute the gap from the per-item JSONL and show the inspection notes; Claude asks for one concrete failing sample and its category

questions.q: A reader cannot reproduce your headline number from the README command; they get 2 pts lower. What do you check, in order?
good_answer: The git SHA and config hash in the results row versus what the command actually runs
Chat template (thinking off) and decoding config (T, top-p, top-k, max tokens): does the eval path use the eval-only truncated sampler as logged?
Sampler version and sampling seed, and whether 2 pts is within the noise floor measured over 3 sampling seeds
Verifier version and timeouts (a slower CPU can time out more), and the item ID lists in data/splits.json
Allocator settings and hardware, then diff the per-item JSONL to find which items changed

Running arms on unbalanced hardware, or dropping a diverged seed after the fact
